"Powerful AI" is defined operationally: smarter than a Nobel laureate across most fields; full virtual interfaces including "mouse and keyboard control, and internet access"; can be "given tasks that take hours, days, or weeks"; no embodiment but "can control existing physical tools, robots, or laboratory equipment through a computer"; "millions of instances" running at "10x-100x human speed" — "a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter'."
evidence.figures: 50–100 years of progress compressed into 5–10 years. ≥10x rate multiplier on tool-discoveries. ~1 major tool discovery per year today, driving >50% of progress in biology. Explicit rejection of 100 years in 1 year; openness to 1000 years in 5–10. Health outcomes dated "7-12 years from now" = 2031–2036 from an October 2024 publication date. Clock start assumed "as early as 2026".
sources: https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/machines-of-loving-grace (Dario Amodei, "Machines of Loving Grace", October 2024 — full text retrieved and read 2026-08-20)
evidence.uncertainty: None on the wording; I read the full primary text. The one interpretive step is dating "7-12 years from now" to 2031–2036 — the essay says October 2024 at the top, so this is arithmetic, but Amodei never writes those calendar years himself.

evidence.question: What are the five areas, and how confident is the essay in each?
evidence.answer:
Verbatim list: "Biology and physical health / Neuroscience and mental health / Economic development and poverty / Peace and governance / Work and meaning."

The confidence gradient across them is steep and explicit, and this matters more for the axis than the list does. Areas 1 and 2 are asserted; areas 3, 4 and 5 are hedged, and area 4 is close to a negative prediction.

Area 3: "I am not as confident that AI can address inequality and economic growth as I am that it can invent fundamental technologies, because technology has such obvious high returns to intelligence... whereas the economy involves a lot of constraints from humans, as well as a large dose of intrinsic complexity." And: "keep in mind everywhere that success is not guaranteed and depends on our collective efforts."

Area 4: "Unfortunately, I see no strong reason to believe AI will preferentially or structurally advance democracy and peace, in the same way that I think it will structurally advance human health and alleviate poverty. Human conflict is adversarial and AI can in principle help both the 'good guys' and the 'bad guys'. If anything, some structural factors seem worrying: AI seems likely to enable much better propaganda and surveillance... the triumph of liberal democracy and political stability is not guaranteed, perhaps not even likely."

Area 5: "I think this question is more difficult than the others... the brevity of this section is not at all to be taken as a sign that I don't take these issues seriously — on the contrary, it is a sign of a lack of clear answers." He concedes "in the long run AI will become so broadly effective and so cheap that this [comparative advantage] will no longer apply. At that point our current economic setup will no longer make sense."

So: the essay is a strong claim about invention (areas 1–2), a hedged claim about distribution (area 3), an explicitly non-claim about governance (area 4), and an admission of no answer about work (area 5). Any axis that treats "Machines of Loving Grace" as a single monolithic optimistic position is misreading it — the essay itself already separates invention from realisation, and is far less confident about realisation.
evidence.figures: Five areas. Sub-Saharan Africa GDP per capita ~$2,000 vs United States ~$75,000 (the essay's own framing figure for area 3). Dream-scenario 20% annual GDP growth in the developing world (10% from AI-enabled economic decisions, 10% from natural spread of technology), which he calls "a dream scenario, not what happens by default".
evidence.uncertainty: None — direct quotation. Note that in his January 2026 essay he re-characterises the growth claim as "a 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth rate may be possible", which is a slightly different framing from the essay's "dream scenario" of 20% in the developing world specifically.

evidence.question: What specific diseases and outcomes does the essay name, with what numbers?
evidence.answer:
The essay's list, with its own hedges attached (the hedges are usually stripped off in quotation, and the reader should have them):

1. "Reliable prevention and treatment of nearly all natural infectious disease." Hedge in footnote: fast-evolving multidrug-resistant strains "could be the kind of thing that prevents us from getting to 100%." Also: "Whether infectious disease is fully eradicated from the world (as opposed to just in some places) depends on questions about poverty and inequality."

2. "Elimination of most cancer." Basis: "Death rates from cancer have been dropping ~2% per year for the last few decades; thus we are on track to eliminate most cancer in the 21st century at the current pace of human science." Target: "Reductions of 95% or more in both mortality and incidence seem possible." Hedge: "cancer is extremely varied and adaptive, and is likely the hardest of these diseases to fully destroy. It would not be surprising if an assortment of rare, difficult malignancies persists."

3. "Very effective prevention and effective cures for genetic disease" via embryo screening plus "some safer, more reliable descendant of CRISPR". Hedge: "Whole-body afflictions that affect a large fraction of cells may be the last holdouts."

4. "Prevention of Alzheimer's." Hedge: "damage from already existing Alzheimer's may be very difficult to reverse."

5. "Improved treatment of most other ailments" — diabetes, obesity, heart disease, autoimmune. Cites "deaths from heart disease have already declined over 50%" and GLP-1 agonists.

6. "Biological freedom" — "weight, physical appearance, reproduction, and other biological processes will be fully under people's control."

7. "Doubling of the human lifespan." Basis: "life expectancy increased almost 2x in the 20th century (from ~40 years to ~75), so it's 'on trend' that the 'compressed 21st' would double it again to 150." Supporting data: "there already exist drugs that increase maximum lifespan in rats by 25-50%"; some turtles live 200 years. Stated prerequisite: "the most important thing that is needed might be reliable, non-Goodhart-able biomarkers of human aging, as that will allow fast iteration on experiments and clinical trials." And a measurement hedge in footnote 18 that is directly on point for a realisation axis: "Note it may be hard to know that we have doubled the human lifespan within the 5-10 years. While we might have accomplished it, we may not know it yet within the study time frame."

Neuroscience: "Most mental illness can probably be cured" — naming "PTSD, depression, schizophrenia, addiction". "Conditions that are very 'structural' may be more difficult, but not impossible" (psychopathy, some intellectual disabilities). "Effective genetic prevention of mental illness seems possible" via embryo screening. Explicitly excluded from the window: mind uploading "faces significant technological and societal challenges, even with powerful AI, that likely put it outside the 5-10 year window."
evidence.figures: Cancer: mortality and incidence reductions of "95% or more"; baseline ~2%/yr decline in death rates. Lifespan: doubling to ~150; 20th-century precedent ~40 → ~75 years; rat maximum-lifespan drugs +25–50%. Heart disease deaths already down >50%. Infectious disease: "nearly all" natural, not 100%.
evidence.uncertainty: None on the text. Note the list is prefaced by "This is not based on any rigorous methodology, and will almost certainly prove wrong in the details, but it's trying to get across the general level of radicalism we should expect" — the numbers are order-of-magnitude signals, not forecasts, by the author's own statement.

evidence.question: What bottlenecks does the essay itself concede? (The reader should know Amodei has already conceded most of the case against him.)
evidence.answer:
The essay's central analytic device is a taxonomy of five limiting factors on "the marginal returns to intelligence", all quoted verbatim:

1. "Speed of the outside world. ... Cells and animals run at a fixed speed so experiments on them take a certain amount of time which may be irreducible. ... in science many experiments are often needed in sequence, each learning from or building on the last. All of this means that the speed at which a major project—for example developing a cancer cure—can be completed may have an irreducible minimum that cannot be decreased further even as intelligence continues to increase."
2. "Need for data. Sometimes raw data is lacking and in its absence more intelligence does not help."
3. "Intrinsic complexity. Some things are inherently unpredictable or chaotic" (the three-body problem).
4. "Constraints from humans. Many things cannot be done without breaking laws, harming humans, or messing up society. ... Examples of advances that work well in a technical sense, but whose impact has been substantially reduced by regulations or misplaced fears, include nuclear power, supersonic flight, and even elevators."
5. "Physical laws. ... Pudding does not unstir."

On clinical trials specifically he concedes the arithmetic but argues the delay is tolerable: "mRNA vaccines for COVID were approved in 9 months—much faster than the usual pace. That said, even under these conditions clinical trials are still too slow—mRNA vaccines arguably should have been approved in ~2 months. But these kinds of delays (~1 year end-to-end for a drug) combined with massive parallelization and the need for some but not too much iteration ('a few tries') are very compatible with radical transformation in 5-10 years." Note what this assumes: that trial slowness is mostly an artefact of weak drugs ("a lot... of their slowness ultimately derives from the need to rigorously evaluate drugs that barely work"), so that big effect sizes collapse the timeline. That assumption is the single load-bearing joint of the whole essay and is where every serious critic attacks.

On the irreducible latency: "I think there's an unavoidable constant delay: experiments and hardware design have a certain 'latency' and need to be iterated upon a certain 'irreducible' number of times in order to learn things that can't be deduced logically."

On distribution — the concession most relevant to a realisation axis: "It is one thing to develop a cure for a disease, it is another thing to eradicate the disease from the world." His own realisation target is explicitly partial: "Overall, I think 5-10 years is a reasonable timeline for a good fraction (maybe 50%) of AI-driven health benefits to propagate to even the poorest countries in the world. A good goal might be for the developing world 5-10 years after powerful AI to at least be substantially healthier than the developed world is today, even if it continues to lag behind the developed world."

And the opt-out problem: "There could end up being bad feedback cycles where, for example, the people who are least able to make good decisions opt out of the very technologies that improve their decision-making abilities, leading to an ever-increasing gap and even creating a dystopian underclass."

His counter-argument on deployment, which is the essay's optimistic asymmetry: "biomedicine is unique in that although the process of developing drugs is overly cumbersome, once developed they generally are successfully deployed and used." That claim is empirically contestable and is contradicted by the access data below.
evidence.figures: Five named limiting factors. mRNA COVID vaccines: 9 months actual, "~2 months" in his view achievable. Assumed steady-state "~1 year end-to-end for a drug". Realisation target: "maybe 50%" of AI-driven health benefits reaching the poorest countries within 5–10 years — i.e. the essay's own best case leaves roughly half unrealised in the poorest countries at the end of the window.
sources: https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/machines-of-loving-grace (October 2024), "Basic assumptions and framework" and Sections 1 and 3
evidence.uncertainty: None on the quotations. The "maybe 50%" figure is a goal he sets, not a prediction he defends, and he attaches "Accomplishing this will of course require a huge effort in global health, philanthropy, political advocacy".

evidence.question: Who argues the constraints bind harder, on what grounds, with what figures?
evidence.answer:
Four distinct lines of published disagreement, which should be kept separate because they imply different axis positions.

A. THE BOTTLENECK IS BIOPHYSICAL, NOT COGNITIVE. Niko McCarty, "Levers for Biological Progress", Asimov Press, 1 November 2024 — the most direct published response. Argument: "most bottlenecks slowing biology today are biophysical rather than computational." Figures cited: DNA cloning takes up to a week; E. coli divides every 20 minutes and human cells about once a day; synthesising a human protein-coding gene costs several hundred dollars; DNA synthesis fell from ~$20/base in 2000 to ~$0.10 today and needs "another 100x"; E. coli has ~4,400 protein-coding genes and is still not fully understood; >500,000 life-sciences researchers in the US would benefit from 10% improvements in common methods; E11 Bio aims to cut whole-mouse-brain connectomics from ~$10bn to under $100m. The implication is not that Amodei is wrong about returns to intelligence but that the tool-building must come first and is itself gated by physical iteration. Stephen Malina's reply ("Riffing on Machines of Loving Grace", 27 December 2024) partly defends Amodei, arguing some of McCarty's bottlenecks are more surmountable and that the capability frontier will be "more jagged" than Amodei assumes.

B. THE BOTTLENECK IS PREDICTIVE VALIDITY, AND MORE IDEAS MAKE IT WORSE. This is the strongest quantitative case against the essay and Amodei does not address it. Scannell & Bosley, "When Quality Beats Quantity: Decision Theory, Drug Discovery, and the Reproducibility Crisis", PLoS ONE, February 2016. Finding: "an 0.1 absolute change in correlation coefficient between model output and clinical outcomes... can offset large (e.g., 10 fold, even 100 fold) changes in models' brute-force efficiency." Their illustration: a single classifier at r=0.9 needs 14 candidates screened per true positive; at r=0.7, 33; at r=0.6, 70. The consequence for the compressed-century thesis is direct — a 10x increase in the rate of generating candidates and hypotheses is worth less than a 0.1 improvement in how well preclinical models predict human outcomes, and AI has so far demonstrated the former far more clearly than the latter. Scannell's follow-up (Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2022) makes predictive validity the dominant variable in R&D productivity. Background: Eroom's Law — new molecular entities approved per billion dollars of inflation-adjusted R&D has halved roughly every nine years since the 1950s; development cost per approved drug is ~100x the 1950s figure in real terms, with 10–15 years to market and $1–3bn per drug.

C. THE BOTTLENECK IS CLINICAL VALIDATION, AND DISCOVERY WAS NEVER THE CONSTRAINT. Abhishaike Mahajan, "AI After Drug Development", Asterisk Magazine issue 13, January 2026: "It is very rare that we don't have enough interesting ideas at the very beginning. Rather, the problem is that testing each one of those ideas is enormously expensive." He cites ~95% failure in oncology and argues that pulling it to 70% would transform the economics; and that Alzheimer's trials "can take decades to reach their primary endpoint". His prescription — patient stratification and clinical-stage ML rather than better molecule generation — is a direct inversion of Amodei's "virtual biologist" framing. Baseline for comparison: BIO/Informa/QLS, "Clinical Development Success Rates 2011–2020" (2021), 12,728 phase transitions across 9,704 programmes and 1,779 companies: likelihood of approval from Phase I = 7.9% overall (5.7% small molecules, 9.1% biologics, 9.7% vaccines).

D. THE BOTTLENECK IS DIFFUSION, AND IT IS MEASURED IN DECADES. Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor, "AI as Normal Technology", Knight First Amendment Institute, April 2025: "the impact of AI is materialized not when methods and capabilities improve, but when those improvements are translated into applications and are diffused through productive sectors of the economy", and in several domains "AI diffusion lags decades behind innovation", with safety validation named as a principal reason. Their historical anchor is electrification — dynamos "everywhere but in the productivity statistics" for roughly 40 years. Daron Acemoglu, "The Simple Macroeconomics of AI" (NBER w32487, May 2024; Economic Policy, 2025): total factor productivity gain of no more than 0.66% over ten years, and under 0.53% once hard-to-learn tasks are weighted — roughly 0.064 percentage points a year. Set against Amodei's 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth, the published range on the same object spans more than two orders of magnitude. For contrast within the mainstream: Goldman Sachs ~1.5% annual US productivity uplift over a decade; McKinsey 1.5–3.4 percentage points on annual GDP growth in advanced economies.

E. THE DIRECT REBUTTAL. Gary Marcus, "No, Dario Amodei, we will not be curing cancer and 'most human disease' in five to ten years", Marcus on AI, 17 August 2026 — written four days ago, responding to Amodei's X thread of 16 August 2026. Grounds assembled from named researchers: Catharine Young — cancer "is more than 200 distinct diseases, all with different causes, biology and mechanisms"; Lior Pachter — "We don't even know what all the human diseases are"; Keith Robison — "proving we can trust it is clever takes preclinical & clinical work, which eats that timeline"; Ethan Mollick on the gap between invention and "actual trials & proof & FDA approval". Marcus's own anchor is that after more than a decade of AI drug discovery no AI-designed drug has reached clinical adoption.
evidence.figures: Scannell & Bosley 2016: Δr = 0.1 offsets a 10–100x throughput change; 14 / 33 / 70 candidates per true positive at r = 0.9 / 0.7 / 0.6. Eroom's Law: NMEs per real $bn halving every ~9 years since the 1950s; ~100x real cost increase vs the 1950s; 10–15 years and $1–3bn per drug. BIO 2021: 7.9% Phase I likelihood of approval (5.7% small molecule / 9.1% biologic / 9.7% vaccine), n=12,728 transitions. Acemoglu: ≤0.66% TFP over 10 years, <0.53% on the harder-task weighting, ~0.064pp/yr. Goldman ~1.5%/yr productivity; McKinsey +1.5–3.4pp GDP growth. McCarty: DNA synthesis $20/base (2000) → ~$0.10 (2024), wants another 100x; E. coli ~4,400 genes; >500,000 US life-science researchers; connectomics $10bn → <$100m target. Mahajan: ~95% oncology failure rate; 70% as the transformative threshold.
sources: https://www.asimov.press/p/levers (Niko McCarty, "Levers for Biological Progress", Asimov Press, 1 Nov 2024)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-022-00552-x (Scannell et al., "Predictive validity in drug discovery", Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2022)
https://www.nber.org/papers/w32487 (Acemoglu, "The Simple Macroeconomics of AI", NBER, May 2024)
evidence.uncertainty: The Scannell figures for r = 0.9/0.7/0.6 come from Figure 5 of the paper as summarised on fetch; I did not read the figure caption directly and the exact framing (single classifier vs multi-step) should be checked before quoting the three numbers together. Acemoglu's estimate is contested on its own terms — Maxwell Tabarrok and Goldman Sachs have both published rebuttals arguing the Hulten's-theorem framing understates general-purpose-technology effects; present it as one end of a range, not as the consensus. The BIO 10.5-year average development duration figure that is often cited alongside 7.9% did not appear in the search result and I have not verified it; use only the 7.9%.

evidence.question: What is the measured state of realised benefit as of August 2026 — the gap between demonstrated capability and anyone actually being better off?
evidence.answer:
BIOMEDICINE. As of August 2026, no drug discovered end-to-end by an AI platform has been approved by the FDA anywhere. The most advanced candidate is Insilico Medicine's rentosertib (ISM001-055), a TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase IIa results published in Nature Medicine on 3 June 2025 (GENESIS-IPF, 71 patients, 22 sites in China, 12 weeks). Primary endpoint was safety and was met; the efficacy signal was secondary — mean FVC change +98.4 mL at 60 mg QD against a mean decline of −20.3 mL on placebo. Phase III registered 7 July 2026 (320 patients, 47 centres in China); FDA Fast Track granted 29 July 2026. So the flagship case, twelve years into AI drug discovery, is one molecule with a 71-patient secondary-endpoint signal now entering the phase where 60% of drugs die.

The phase profile is the crux. AI-derived molecules show 80–90% Phase I success against a historical 50–65% (Jayatunga et al., Drug Discovery Today, 2024), but ~40% in Phase II — indistinguishable from the industry baseline. Phase I asks whether humans tolerate a molecule; Phase II asks whether it changes a disease. AI has moved the first number and not the second. Published caveats on the Phase I figure: the denominator is a few dozen molecules; and companies plausibly select targets where safety is easier to predict, which inflates it.

Against that, the field has consumed roughly $60bn since 2019 and Recursion — after absorbing Exscientia in a 2024–25 merger of the two best-capitalised AI drug discovery companies — cut or paused five programmes including three clinical ones (REC-2282, REC-994, REC-3964). REC-994 met its safety primary endpoint over 12 months and showed no meaningful clinical benefit. That is the shape of the gap in one sentence: the capability was demonstrated, the trial was run, the endpoint was met, and no patient was better off.

ECONOMY-WIDE. US nonfarm business labour productivity rose 2.9% over the year to Q1 2026 (BLS, reported 7 May 2026) — a genuine pickup. But the Kansas City Fed's industry decomposition finds the gains are not broad-based: a small set of industries accounts for most of them, and while higher AI adoption correlates with faster productivity growth across industries, it "explains little of the shift in aggregate contributions." Census BTOS for November 2025–January 2026: 18% of firms used AI in a business function, 32% employment-weighted, expected to reach 22% within six months. Adoption is real, concentrated, and running well ahead of measurable diffuse benefit.

ACCESS — WHO RECEIVES, AND WHEN. This is the strongest empirical constraint on the essay's distribution claims and it does not depend on any view about AI at all. Health Affairs, October 2024 (119 essential medicines, 6,871 launches, 75 markets, 1982–2024): median time from first global launch to availability was 2.7 years in high-income countries, 4.5 in upper-middle, 6.9 in lower-middle, and 8.0 years in low-income countries. So the access lag alone, for medicines that already exist, consumes most or all of Amodei's 5–10 year realisation window before AI enters the picture.

And the hepatitis C case is the cleanest natural experiment available on "a cure exists and the gains are not realised": direct-acting antivirals cure >95% of cases and have existed since 2013. WHO Global Hepatitis Report 2024: of people living with chronic hepatitis C, 36% had been diagnosed and 20% (12.5 million) had received curative treatment. Eleven years after the cure, four in five of the people it would cure have not had it. Amodei's counter-claim — "once developed they generally are successfully deployed and used" — is false for the single best modern example of a curative therapy.
evidence.figures: Zero AI-discovered drugs approved as of Aug 2026. Rentosertib: n=71, 12 weeks, FVC +98.4 mL (60 mg) vs −20.3 mL placebo, Nature Medicine 3 Jun 2025; Phase III registered 7 Jul 2026 (320 patients, 47 centres); FDA Fast Track 29 Jul 2026. AI molecules: 80–90% Phase I vs 50–65% historical; ~40% Phase II vs industry baseline. ~$60bn invested in AI drug discovery since 2019. Recursion/Exscientia: five programmes cut or paused. US productivity +2.9% y/y to Q1 2026; +0.8% q/q. Census BTOS: 18% of firms, 32% employment-weighted (Nov 2025–Jan 2026), 22% expected within six months. Health Affairs 2024: median years to availability 2.7 / 4.5 / 6.9 / 8.0 by income group. WHO 2024: HCV 36% diagnosed, 20% treated (12.5m), against an 80% treatment target for 2030.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S135964462400134X (Jayatunga et al., "How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials?", Drug Discovery Today, 2024)
evidence.uncertainty: The rentosertib placebo comparator is reported inconsistently across secondary sources: the Insilico/Nature Medicine release gives −20.3 mL, while several aggregator sites give −62.3 mL. Use −20.3 mL and cite the release, or read the paper. The "$60bn since 2019" and "173 programmes in clinical development" figures come only from SEO-grade aggregator sites and I could not source them primarily — treat as indicative, do not print. evidence.question: Has Amodei updated, retracted or restated the thesis since October 2024?
evidence.answer:
He has never retracted it, has restated it repeatedly, and has twice made material changes that are easy to miss because the headline number never moves.

CHANGE 1 — THE CLOCK START SLIPPED, WHICH MOVES EVERY OUTCOME DATE. October 2024: powerful AI "could come as early as 2026", and the 5–10 year clock starts there. January 2026, "The Adolescence of Technology": "powerful AI could be as little as 1–2 years away, although it could also be considerably further out." That is 2027–2028, not 2026. The compressed-century outcomes therefore move from a 2031–2036 window to roughly 2032–2038 on his own arithmetic, without a single number in the thesis changing. A forecast keyed to the headline "5–10 years" inherits a start date that has already moved by two years.

CHANGE 2 — HE SEPARATED CAPABILITY FROM CONSEQUENCE, EXPLICITLY. Footnote in the January 2026 essay: "even if powerful AI is only 1–2 years away in a technical sense, many of its societal consequences, both positive and negative, may take a few years longer to occur. This is why I can simultaneously think that AI will disrupt 50% of entry-level white-collar jobs over 1–5 years, while also thinking we may have AI that is more capable than everyone in only 1–2 years." This is Amodei himself asserting that the reader's proposed axis is a distinct quantity from capability tempo.

THE SUBSTANTIVE WALK-BACK, JULY 2026. At the Claude Science launch, on stage, reported by Matthew Herper, STAT News, 6 July 2026: "I don't think that today we can make progress at a rate of 10 years per year for a number of reasons" — naming three: models are not yet good enough; researchers need time to learn to use the tools; and "the infrastructure and regulatory systems will take time to change." Herper reports that Amodei said his original vision "might not start to be visible for a decade." That is the most important single sentence for this axis in the whole record: not that the gains arrive in 5–10 years, but that they might not begin to be visible for ten. The two other named causes are diffusion (learning to use the tools) and institutions (infrastructure and regulation) — neither of which is a capability variable.

RESTATEMENT WITHOUT REVISION, JANUARY 2026. The Adolescence of Technology keeps the thesis intact and conditional: "We will likely get a 'century of scientific and economic progress compressed into a decade,' and this will be hugely positive for the world, but we will then have to contend with the problems that arise from this rapid rate of progress." It appears in the section on unknown unknowns — the compressed century is now framed partly as a risk vector.

MOST RECENT, 16 AUGUST 2026 — four days ago. In a two-part reply on X to investor Gavin Baker (reportedly 14m+ views), Amodei restated that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in around five to ten years, while conceding that AI companies including his own "haven't yet delivered" on what they promised, and promising "early glimmers" of medical results "in the coming months". He also wrote that "saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive," and that "actually curing it is the only thing that works." This is the proximate cause of the Gary Marcus rebuttal of 17 August 2026.

INSTITUTIONAL FOLLOW-THROUGH. Anthropic launched Claude Science on 30 June 2026 — an AI workbench for scientists, 60+ curated skills and connectors across genomics, proteomics, structural biology and cheminformatics — and announced it will run its own preclinical drug-discovery programmes focused on neglected and rare diseases, with a stated ambition to compress life-sciences R&D timelines tenfold. The named results so far are throughput results, not outcome results: a UCSF epidemiologist reporting germline workups "in roughly one-tenth the time it previously took", and an Allen Institute neuroscientist completing ~10 literature reviews of 100+ pages where the work "could take as many as two years". These are exactly the capability-side demonstrations the axis needs to distinguish from realised benefit.

evidence.question: What is genuinely contested, and what is the range?
evidence.answer:
Five things are contested, and on each the published range is wide enough that the axis needs to carry the spread rather than a point estimate.

1. WHETHER DISCOVERY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AT ALL. Amodei says yes and that returns to intelligence are high there. Mahajan (Asterisk, Jan 2026) and Scannell (2016, 2022) say the binding constraint is the predictive validity of the models used to decide what to test, and that raising idea throughput without raising validity makes the funnel worse, not better. McCarty (Nov 2024) says it is neither — it is the physical tools. These are three different theories of the bottleneck and they imply three different axis positions, not three degrees of one position.

2. WHETHER LARGE EFFECT SIZES COLLAPSE TRIAL TIMELINES. This is the load-bearing joint. Amodei: trial slowness "ultimately derives from the need to rigorously evaluate drugs that barely work", so big effects give "~1 year end-to-end". Against: the BIO 7.9% Phase I likelihood of approval is over a decade in which effect size varied enormously; oncology failure remains ~95%; Alzheimer's endpoints take years to decades regardless of mechanism; and the one AI-designed drug with a Phase II efficacy signal took from 2021 to 2026 to get from candidate to Phase III. No one has published a clean test of Amodei's claim, and it is testable — the honest position is that it is unresolved.

3. THE MACROECONOMIC MAGNITUDE. Acemoglu ≤0.66% TFP over ten years; Goldman ~1.5% annual productivity; McKinsey +1.5–3.4pp on GDP growth; Amodei 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth. That is a spread of more than two orders of magnitude on the same quantity, published in the same three years, by people who have all seen the same evidence. Current measurement is ambiguous in a way that supports neither end: US productivity +2.9% y/y to Q1 2026, but the Kansas City Fed finds the gains concentrated in a few industries and largely unexplained by AI adoption.

4. WHETHER THE PHASE I RESULT MEANS ANYTHING. 80–90% vs 50–65% is a real difference on the published data, and it is also exactly what you would expect from a few dozen molecules chosen partly for predictable safety. Both readings are live. What is not contested is that Phase II is unchanged at ~40%.

5. WHETHER DEPLOYMENT IS THE EASY PART. Amodei asserts biomedicine deploys reliably once developed. The access data say otherwise: 8.0-year median to availability in low-income countries, and 20% treatment coverage for a hepatitis C cure that has existed since 2013. I found no published defence of Amodei's deployment asymmetry against those figures — he asserts it, and the counter-evidence is not obscure.

WHAT IS NOT CONTESTED: that no AI-discovered drug has been approved anywhere as of August 2026; that Phase II success for AI-derived molecules matches the industry baseline; that Amodei himself said in July 2026 that a 10-years-per-year rate is not achievable today; and that the essay's own aggressive-case date for its disease list is 2031–2036.

Phase I: 80–90% (AI) vs 50–65% (historical), n = a few dozen. Phase II: ~40% both. Access: 2.7 / 4.5 / 6.9 / 8.0 median years by income group. HCV: 36% diagnosed, 20% treated, cure available since 2013.
evidence.uncertainty: The Goldman and McKinsey figures came via search summary of an AEI article rather than the primary reports; verify before printing. On point 5, absence of a published defence is my finding from searching, not proof that none exists.

evidence.question: What should the new axis's positions actually differ on, given this evidence?
evidence.answer:
The evidence separates cleanly into four independent quantities, and a position on the axis should be a combination of them rather than a point on a single optimism-to-pessimism line. Naming them stops the axis from being a duplicate of T or D.

WHICH DOMAIN LANDS FIRST. The record does not support a single ordering. Software and scientific throughput are already realised (one-tenth-time germline workups; two-year literature reviews compressed). Biomedicine has demonstrated candidate generation and Phase I tolerability but not changed disease course. Logistics and materials sit between. A domain-ordering that runs software → science-throughput → logistics → clinical outcome → population health is defensible from the data; the essay assumes clinical outcome arrives near the front, and its author no longer says that.

WHAT GATES IT. Four distinct gates appear in the literature and they bind at different times: (i) physical iteration latency — cell division, animal studies, chemistry; (ii) predictive validity — whether preclinical models predict humans, where a 0.1 change in r beats a 100x throughput change; (iii) institutional throughput — trials, regulators, procurement, reimbursement, clinician adoption; (iv) distribution and payment — who pays, in which country, at what price. Position (ii) is the one no forecast currently carries and it is the one with the hardest published number attached.

WHO RECEIVES. The access data give a ready-made scale that owes nothing to any AI assumption: high-income first, then upper-middle at +1.8 years, lower-middle at +4.2, low-income at +5.3 (medians from first global launch: 2.7 / 4.5 / 6.9 / 8.0). And the hepatitis C figures show that even within a receiving country the realised fraction can sit at 20% eleven years after the cure exists. A position that says "the cure exists and the median person who needs it does not have it" is a real, observed world, not a pessimistic scenario.

HOW LONG THE LAG RUNS BETWEEN CAPABILITY AND A PERSON BEING BETTER OFF. The published anchors span roughly a decade and a half: Amodei's own 5–10 years post-powerful-AI; his July 2026 statement that it "might not start to be visible for a decade"; the essay's own 2031–2036 dating; the electrification precedent at ~40 years; the essential-medicines access lag at 2.7–8.0 years for things already invented; and Narayanan and Kapoor's "decades" for safety-critical domains. A lag axis with positions at roughly 3, 8, 15 and 30+ years from capability to measurable population benefit would span the published range without inventing anything.

ONE STRUCTURAL POINT WORTH BUILDING IN. Amodei's January 2026 footnote — capability in 1–2 years, societal consequence "a few years longer" — and his July 2026 remark that models, researcher learning and "infrastructure and regulatory systems" are the three brakes, together mean the author of the reference text now holds that realisation is a separate variable from capability with its own clock. The axis is not arguing with him about that. It is measuring the thing he says exists.

And for the reader's specific complaint about the 2036 headline: the two sentences are not in tension once the quantities are separated. "The machines keep getting better" is a T statement. "Wrong in ways found on the factory floor" is a statement about realised benefit under institutional gating — and Amodei's own dating puts the compressed-century disease list at 2031–2036, with his July 2026 revision pushing the start of visibility to about 2036. A 2036 world in which capability is high, benefits are real in throughput terms, and the clinical and population gains are only beginning to show is not the pessimistic corner of this axis. It is close to the reference text's own aggressive case, re-dated by its author.
evidence.figures: Access ladder: +0 / +1.8 / +4.2 / +5.3 years by income group (from medians 2.7 / 4.5 / 6.9 / 8.0). Realised fraction within a receiving population: 20% (HCV treatment, 11 years post-cure). Lag anchors for positions: ~3 / ~8 / ~15 / 30+ years. Predictive validity gate: Δr 0.1 > 100x throughput. Amodei's own re-dating: disease list 2031–2036 (Oct 2024 arithmetic); visibility "a decade" out from July 2026 ≈ 2036.
evidence.uncertainty: This finding is my synthesis for axis design, not a published position — the four quantities are drawn from the sources but no source proposes this decomposition. The suggested lag anchors (3/8/15/30+) are constructed to span the published range and are not themselves a published set. Treat the decomposition as a proposal to be argued with, and keep the underlying figures, which are sourced.

evidence.question: Who has access to frontier systems today, measured, and how big is the rich–poor gap?
evidence.answer:
The gap in *use* is roughly an order of magnitude larger than the gap in *income*, and two orders larger than the gap in internet access. The World Bank's Atlas of Global Development 2026 (published May 2026) finds that as of May 2025, visits to ChatGPT per internet user were about 50 times greater in high-income than low-income countries, 8x versus lower-middle income, and 3x versus upper-middle income. Note the denominator: this is per *internet user*, so it is a gap on top of the connectivity gap, not the connectivity gap itself. Low-income countries accounted for under 1% of generative-AI traffic. In most sub-Saharan African countries, fewer than 10% of the working-age population uses AI at all. Anthropic's Economic Index geography work finds the same shape from a different vendor's data: a 1% higher GDP per capita is associated with roughly 0.7% higher Claude use per capita across countries; Singapore runs at 4.6x its population share and Canada 2.9x, while Indonesia is 0.36x, India 0.27x and Nigeria 0.2x. The World Bank Atlas reports Claude usage in lower-prosperity countries about 10x below high-income levels.

The physical substrate is more concentrated still. As of June 2025 the World Bank puts 77% of global data-centre capacity in high-income countries, 23% in middle-income, and under 0.1% in low-income countries. The United States has roughly 20,000 times as many servers per capita as low-income nations and 200 times as many as middle-income ones. Africa holds under 1% of global data-centre capacity and an estimated 80% of its internet traffic is served from outside the continent, mostly Europe.

Crucially, 'middle-income' and 'low-income' behave completely differently and are routinely conflated. Brazil, India, Indonesia and Vietnam drove more than 40% of ChatGPT traffic by mid-2025; the World Development Report 2026 notes middle-income countries reached half of ChatGPT's global traffic within six months of launch. Low-income countries did not. Any axis that treats 'the global south' as one bucket will get this wrong.

May 2026). vs lower-middle income 8x; vs upper-middle income 3x. Low-income share of GenAI traffic: <1% (World Bank). Sub-Saharan Africa: <10% of working-age population uses AI in most countries (World Bank, 2026). GDP elasticity of Claude use per capita across countries: 0.7 (Anthropic Economic Index, geography report). Per-capita usage index: Singapore 4.6x, Canada 2.9x, Indonesia 0.36x, India 0.27x, Nigeria 0.2x (Anthropic, 2026). US share of global Claude use: 21.6%. Data-centre capacity June 2025: high-income 77%, middle-income 23%, low-income <0.1%; US servers per capita 20,000x low-income, 200x middle-income (World Bank). Africa <1% of global data-centre capacity; ~80% of African internet traffic served offshore. Basic digital skills in low-income countries: 5% of population (2023, World Bank). Middle-income share of ChatGPT traffic within 6 months of launch: 50% (WDR 2026, pub. Aug 2026); >40% of global traffic from middle-income countries mid-2025.

The 50x figure is a May 2025 snapshot and is now ~15 months stale; free-tier deals in India since Oct 2025 will have moved the India component sharply. The Anthropic index measures a product with an enterprise/developer skew, so its country ranking is not a general-population AI-use ranking.

evidence.question: Is the access gap widening or narrowing? What is the honest range?
evidence.answer:
This is genuinely contested, and the contest is mostly about which quantity is being measured. In *growth rates off a small base*, the poorest countries are catching up fast: OpenAI's own usage research reports that by May 2025 ChatGPT adoption growth in the lowest-income countries was over 4x that in the highest-income countries. In *levels*, the gap is enormous and closing slowly or not at all. And on at least one recent measure it is widening: Daepp and Slaughter (arXiv 2605.30685, 29 May 2026) find that by the second half of 2025, adoption was growing *twice as fast in the Global North as in the Global South* — a direct reversal of the earlier picture. Anthropic's index finds global concentration *increased*, with the top 20 countries rising from 45% to 48% of per-capita usage; within the US, states are converging but at a rate implying rough parity in 5–9 years rather than 2–5.

The two claims are reconcilable — a low base can grow fast in percentage terms while the absolute gap grows — which is exactly why an axis should not be keyed to 'is the gap closing'. It should be keyed to levels and to a dated threshold. On levels, the ordering has been stable since 2023: high-income → upper-middle → lower-middle → low-income, with roughly an order of magnitude between the ends.

Separately, the language gap is a persistent multiplier: countries whose languages are well represented in training data adopt at roughly twice the rate, and model quality itself is stratified — MMLU-ProX scores average 64.6 for the Americas/Europe, 58.1 Asia/Oceania, 41.3 Africa. A user in Lagos is not getting the same model as a user in London even when both type into the same box.
evidence.figures: Growth rate, lowest-income vs highest-income countries: >4x (by May 2025, OpenAI usage research). Growth in H2 2025: Global North growing 2x as fast as Global South (Daepp & Slaughter, arXiv 2605.30685, 29 May 2026). Low-income share of GenAI website visits, March 2024: <1%. Adoption rate, Global North 25% vs Global South 14% (2026 reporting). Concentration: top 20 countries rose 45%→48% of per-capita Claude usage; US top-5 states fell 30%→24% Aug 2025–Feb 2026, implying parity in 5–9 years (Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026 report). Language effect: ~2x higher adoption where the national language is well represented in training data. Model quality by region, MMLU-ProX: Americas/Europe 64.6, Asia/Oceania 58.1, Africa 41.3. IMF (Jan 2024): job exposure to AI 60% advanced economies, 40% emerging markets, 26% low-income countries. UNCTAD Technology and Innovation Report 2025: 100 firms, mostly US and China, accounted for 40% of global AI R&D in 2022; 118 countries absent from leading AI governance forums; 1 in 3 developing countries has an AI strategy vs 2 in 3 developed.
evidence.uncertainty: The two directional claims come from different vendors, different denominators (visits vs users vs per-capita index) and different windows, and neither has been independently replicated. Nobody has a clean panel of *individual* AI use by income group over time; everything is inferred from traffic or from one company's logs. The Daepp & Slaughter reversal is a single preprint from May 2026 and is the least corroborated figure in this whole set — treat the direction as unresolved, not as established.

evidence.question: What is actually deployed in low-income health systems, and what has it delivered in outcomes?
evidence.answer:
Deployment is real but narrow, and the evidence base for benefit is nearly empty. The hardest number in the field: of 86 randomised clinical trials of AI health tools conducted anywhere in the world between 2018 and 2023, only four took place in low- or middle-income countries. That is the state of knowledge on which the Gates Foundation, Wellcome and the Novo Nordisk Foundation launched the $60M Evidence for AI in Health (EVAH) initiative on 20 February 2026 — an initiative whose existence is itself the finding: in 2026 the major funders are still paying to discover whether these tools work in poor health systems.

What exists at scale is chest-X-ray triage for tuberculosis. WHO has recommended computer-aided detection (CAD) for TB screening since 2021 and in June 2025 doubled the list of recommended products from four to eight. The largest vendor reports deployment at ~2,658 sites across 90 countries and around 2.5 million people screened worldwide in 2023. Set that against the denominator: WHO's Global TB Report 2025 estimates 10.7 million incident TB cases in 2024, of which 2.3–2.4 million were never diagnosed or reported. A tool operating at ~2.5 million screens a year is a real intervention against a gap of ~2.4 million missed cases, but it is a triage aid, not a cure, and it has not moved the aggregate: TB incidence is down only 12% and mortality 29% since 2015, against End TB milestones of −50% and −75%.

The best-evidenced LLM deployment is a clinical safety net in Kenya: across 39,849 visits at 15 clinics January–April 2025, AI Consult reduced diagnostic errors 16% and treatment errors 13% (31% where the system actually flagged something). Note what that measures — clinician error rates judged by other clinicians. Not mortality, not morbidity, not a day of life gained. The first published randomised trial of a health AI intervention in Nigeria (SPEC-AI) doubled detection of cardiomyopathy in obstetric patients: again detection, not outcome, and in a setting where the treatment following detection may not be available.

This process-versus-outcome substitution is systematic, not incidental: the Lancet Digital Health noted in 2026 that RCTs of AI in healthcare overwhelmingly report process measures (accuracy, detection rate, time-to-result, workflow efficiency) rather than mortality, morbidity or quality of life, and that the effect on patient-relevant outcomes remains uncertain.

The canonical failure case is still instructive. When a diabetic-retinopathy screening model with better-than-specialist lab accuracy was deployed prospectively in 11 Thai clinics (2018–19), it rejected 21% of ~1,840 nurse-captured images as too low quality — mostly because the clinics had no room that could be darkened — and slow broadband meant nurses screened about 10 patients per two-hour session. Nothing was wrong with the model.

Largest CAD vendor: ~2,658 sites, 90 countries; ~2.5M screened worldwide in 2023, >1M in Africa. The Penda study is non-randomised (staggered rollout, clinic-level comparison) and was conducted with the model provider as co-author. The '86 RCTs, 4 in LMICs' figure is quoted by the Gates Foundation from a Lancet study I could not open directly; the underlying review's inclusion criteria matter a lot and I have not seen them. No source anywhere claims a measured mortality or morbidity benefit from AI at population scale in any low-income country.

evidence.question: Pricing and availability of models in the global south — is price the binding constraint?
evidence.answer:
Price has already collapsed and is not, on current evidence, the binding constraint. Stanford's AI Index found the cost of querying a model at GPT-3.5 level (64.8% MMLU) fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024 — a 280-fold drop in about 18 months. Consumer pricing has followed: ChatGPT Go launched in India at ₹399/month (~$4.50) and was then made free for 12 months for eligible Indian users; Google gave 18 months of its Pro tier free to Reliance Jio subscribers (a bundle nominally worth ~₹35,100), reaching a subscriber base of roughly 500 million. India is now the second-largest ChatGPT market with around 100 million weekly users.

So the marginal price of frontier-adjacent intelligence in a large lower-middle-income market is currently zero, and the gap did not close. That is the important fact. What remains binding, in rough order:

1. **Connectivity and devices.** GSMA (9 Sept 2025): 4.7 billion people use mobile internet (58% of the world); 3.1 billion live under coverage and do not use it (the usage gap, 38% of the world); only ~300 million (4%) have no coverage at all. 93% of the unconnected live in LMICs. An entry-level internet-enabled handset costs 16% of average monthly income in LMICs and 48% of monthly income for the poorest quintile. In sub-Saharan Africa mobile internet penetration was 27% at end-2023 with a 60% usage gap.
2. **Electricity.** 730 million people had no electricity in 2024 (IEA), eight in ten of them in sub-Saharan Africa. Nearly a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lack reliable power and more than two-thirds lack dependable internet (WDR 2026).
3. **Skills.** Only 5% of people in low-income countries had basic digital skills in 2023.
4. **Availability by jurisdiction.** Frontier access is not universal. Anthropic lists 195 supported countries/regions but excludes, among others, the DRC, Afghanistan, Iran, North Korea, Syria and Myanmar; OpenAI's unsupported list includes Afghanistan, Eritrea, South Sudan, Eswatini, Chad, Central African Republic and Yemen. Roughly nine African countries face restricted ChatGPT access.

For scale on the subscription question anyway: the World Bank's low-income ceiling is GNI per capita of $1,175 (2025, FY27 classification) — under $100 a month. A $20/month plan is roughly a fifth of that; a $4.50 plan roughly 5%.
