evidence.question: Has any measured health or productivity gap actually moved because of AI, either between countries or within them?
evidence.answer:
No — not at the level of national statistics, in either direction, anywhere. What exists is a set of trial-level results that point *both ways* on distribution, and a macro literature that cannot yet find the effect at all.

**Evidence that AI narrows gaps.** Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's study of 5,179 customer-support agents found productivity up 14% on average but 34% for novice and low-skilled workers with minimal effect on the most experienced — the mechanism being that the model diffuses the best workers' practice. In Edo State, Nigeria, a six-week after-school programme with GPT-4 produced 0.31 SD on a composite assessment and 0.23 SD on English, described by the World Bank as equivalent to 1.5–2 years of business-as-usual schooling and among the most cost-effective education interventions measured.

**Evidence that AI widens gaps.** Otis et al.'s field experiment with 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs (GPT-4 business assistant over WhatsApp) found high performers gained just over 15% while low performers did about 8% *worse*. The advice given was not different; what differed was the capacity to judge which advice to act on. This is the single most important counter-result for a global-benefits axis, because it shows the same tool, same price, same delivery channel, in the same poor country, increasing within-country inequality. METR's randomised trial found 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% *slower* with early-2025 AI tools on 246 tasks in their own repositories — while believing they had been 20% faster.

**Macro.** Acemoglu's estimate is a TFP gain of no more than 0.66% over ten years, revised down to under 0.53%; Aghion and Bunel and OECD-adjacent work put annual labour-productivity gains up to ~1 percentage point. Most macro studies through 2026 find limited evidence of a significant AI effect in aggregate productivity data. The spread between the low and high credible estimates is roughly tenfold, and that spread is a property of modelling assumptions, not of data.

For the axis: nothing here licenses a claim about who receives the gains. The honest position is that as of August 2026 the distributional sign is unresolved and appears to depend on whether the user already has the judgement to filter the model's output — which is precisely the resource that is unequally distributed.
evidence.figures: Brynjolfsson/Li/Raymond: 5,179 agents; +14% issues resolved per hour overall, +34% for novice/low-skilled, ~0 for the most skilled (NBER w31161). Otis et al., Kenya: 640 entrepreneurs, GPT-4 via WhatsApp; high performers +15%, low performers −8% (Management Science). Nigeria/Edo World Bank RCT (Policy Research WP 11125, May 2025): 9 schools, 6 weeks; +0.31 SD composite, +0.23 SD English; ≈1.5–2 years of business-as-usual schooling. METR RCT (July 2025): 16 developers, 246 tasks, 19% slower with AI; self-estimated 20% faster. Acemoglu: ≤0.66% TFP over 10 years, revised to <0.53%. Aghion & Bunel / Filippucci et al.: ~1pp annual labour-productivity growth. IMF: AI job exposure 60% / 40% / 26% by income group.
evidence.uncertainty: Every one of these is a small, short, single-context trial and none has been replicated in a second country. The Nigeria trial ran six weeks in nine schools with imperfect attendance; the effect may not persist or scale. The Kenya result and the Brynjolfsson result point in opposite directions on the same question and both are credible — the reconciliation (call-centre work has a verifiable right answer and a scripted workflow; running a business does not) is my inference, not a finding either paper establishes. The macro range is model-driven; neither end is falsified by data yet. METR's own follow-up (Feb 2026) says they are changing the experiment design, so treat the −19% as a snapshot of early-2025 tools, not a standing result.

evidence.question: What does 'Machines of Loving Grace' actually claim about global distribution, and what does it concede?
evidence.answer:
The essay (Dario Amodei, October 2024) is much more hedged than its reputation. Its core claim is that AI-enabled biology could compress 50–100 years of progress into 5–10 years after 'powerful AI' arrives — a model 'smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most relevant fields'. Its five areas are biology and physical health; neuroscience and mental health; economic development and poverty; peace and governance; and work and meaning.

On the question this axis asks, it says something specific and testable: **'I think 5-10 years is a reasonable timeline for a good fraction (maybe 50%) of AI-driven health benefits to propagate to even the poorest countries.'** If powerful AI arrives around 2026–27, that puts 50% propagation to the poorest countries at roughly 2031–2037 — squarely inside the window the 2036 headline sits in. That sentence is the single best anchor for calibrating an axis position.

It also concedes almost everything a sceptic would raise. Amodei names five limiting factors: speed of the outside world, need for data, intrinsic complexity, constraints from humans, and physical laws. He treats regulation as a real drag (his benchmark: mRNA vaccines 'arguably *should* have been approved in ~2 months' rather than nine). And on distribution he explicitly downgrades his confidence: 'I am not as confident that AI can address inequality and economic growth.' The 20% annual GDP growth figure in the developing world is offered as 'a dream scenario—perhaps a goal to aim for'—and explicitly 'not what happens by default'. His concerns include corruption in developing institutions, an 'opt-out problem' where people refuse beneficial technologies, and the risk of a 'dystopian underclass'.

The forecast should therefore not treat the essay as an optimistic base rate to argue against. It is a conditional claim with the author's own confidence ordering attached: high on biology, notably lower on distribution, lowest on governance and meaning. The disagreement worth representing is not 'Amodei vs sceptics' but 'the biology claim vs the delivery claim' — and Amodei himself puts them in different confidence tiers.
evidence.figures: Publication: October 2024. Compression claim: 50–100 years of biological progress in 5–10 years. Powerful AI: 'smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most relevant fields'. Propagation to poorest countries: 'maybe 50%' of AI-driven health benefits within 5–10 years. Disease targets within the window: ~95% reduction in cancer mortality and incidence; prevention of Alzheimer's; reliable prevention/treatment of nearly all natural infectious disease; doubling of human lifespan to ~150. Developing-world GDP: 20% annual growth as a 'dream scenario'; sub-Saharan Africa ~$2,000 GDP per capita vs US ~$75,000. Regulatory benchmark: mRNA vaccine approval 9 months actual vs ~2 months claimed achievable. Five limiting factors: speed of the outside world, need for data, intrinsic complexity, constraints from humans, physical laws.
evidence.uncertainty: The essay gives no probability distribution and explicitly disclaims precision ('everything I'm saying could very easily be wrong'; 'many, perhaps most' details will be wrong). The 5–10 year clock starts at 'powerful AI', which is undated, so any calendar year derived from it inherits the T-axis's uncertainty. Whether 'a good fraction (maybe 50%) of AI-driven health benefits' means 50% of benefit magnitude, 50% of interventions, or 50% of people is not specified, and those give very different tests.

evidence.question: What is the historical base rate — how long did other transformative technologies take to reach most of the world?
evidence.answer:
Every clean measurement lands between two and fourteen decades, and the fastest cases were fast because someone paid for delivery, not because the technology was good.

**Electricity.** Pearl Street Station opened 1882. In 1935 only 10.9% of American farms (744,000) had central-station power; by 1945, 40%; by 1960, almost 97% — a 25-year sprint bought by a federal lending programme, and that was inside the richest country in the world. Globally, 730 million people still had no electricity in 2024, 144 years after Pearl Street, eight in ten of them in sub-Saharan Africa, with progress in 2024 of only 11 million people.

**Vaccines.** Jenner 1796 → smallpox eradicated 1980: 184 years. But the *delivery* clock is the useful one: the WHO Intensified Eradication Programme ran 1967–1977 — ten years from campaign start to last endemic case, for a cheap, heat-stable, single-dose intervention with no regulatory obstacle and a global coalition, at ~$23M a year plus $200M from endemic countries. That is the fastest global health delivery in history and it took a decade. For newer vaccines, introduction into low-income countries lagged high-income first use by 10–20 years (Hib, pneumococcal conjugate). And coverage plateaus below universal: in 2025, global DTP3 coverage was 85% and first-dose measles 84%, with 13.5 million zero-dose children — worse than the 12.8 million of 2019.

**Antibiotics.** Penicillin reached mass production in 1943–45. It began reaching Africa in the 1940s but extensive use was not possible until the mid-1950s, and only after deliberate UN/WHO funding of production and training. Eighty years on the access problem is still the larger one: the 2024 Lancet AMR series' central reframing is that *lack of access to antibiotics kills more people than resistance to them*, and that improved access to health care and antibiotics could save 92 million lives between 2025 and 2050.

**Mobile telephony — the fastest case.** First commercial cellular network 1979. Sub-Saharan Africa reached one subscriber per 100 people around 2000 and ~9% penetration in 2004; unique subscribers were forecast at 52% of the population by 2025. Mobile *internet* penetration in sub-Saharan Africa was 27% at end-2023 — 44 years after the technology existed, with a 60% usage gap remaining under coverage.

**Green Revolution — the closest analogue to a knowledge technology.** Adoption of modern crop varieties across developing countries rose from 9% of area in 1970 to 63% in 1998 — 28 years for two-thirds coverage. And sub-Saharan Africa largely missed it: the varieties were location-specific, Asian rice performed poorly in Africa, Mexican maize disappointed under African farm conditions. The technology worked; it did not transfer.

**The World Bank's own framing.** WDR 2026 (August 2026) puts it at about 80 years for the steam engine to reach lower-income countries, 40 for electricity, 20 for the internet — and argues AI is faster, citing middle-income countries reaching half of ChatGPT traffic within six months. That comparison is doing work it cannot bear: half of *traffic* from middle-income countries is not the same event as electricity arriving in a village, and low-income countries were under 1% of that traffic.
evidence.figures: Electricity: Pearl Street 1882; US farms electrified 10.9% (1935, 744,000 farms) → 40% (1945) → ~97% (1960); 730M people without electricity globally in 2024, −11M on 2023, 8 in 10 in sub-Saharan Africa (IEA). Smallpox: Jenner 1796 → eradication declared May 1980 (184 yrs); Intensified Programme 1967 → last endemic case Somalia 26 Oct 1977 (10 yrs); ~$23M/yr 1967–79, $98M international + $200M from endemic countries. Vaccine introduction lag, high- to low-income: 10–20 years (Hib, PCV). WUENIC 2025: DTP3 85%, MCV1 84%, zero-dose children 13.5M (vs 12.8M in 2019), 19.6M under- or unvaccinated. Antibiotics: penicillin mass production 1943–45; extensive African use not possible until mid-1950s; lack of access kills more than resistance (Lancet AMR series 2024); 92M lives saveable 2025–2050 from improved access. Mobile: first commercial cellular 1979; SSA 1 subscriber per 100 people ~2000, 9.1% penetration 2004 (7.3% SSA), unique subscribers 52% of population by 2025; mobile internet penetration 27% end-2023, 60% usage gap. Green Revolution: modern-variety area in developing countries 9% (1970) → 63% (1998); >85% wheat and ~65% rice in Asia and Latin America by 1998; minimal SSA adoption (Evenson & Gollin, Science 2003). WDR 2026: steam ~80 yrs, electricity 40 yrs, internet 20 yrs to reach lower-income countries.
evidence.uncertainty: 'Reaching most of the world' has no standard definition and each technology's natural metric differs (households connected, area planted, subscriptions per 100, coverage percentage), so cross-technology comparison is approximate by construction. The WDR 2026 steam/electricity/internet figures are the Bank's own summary and I have not seen the underlying series or its threshold definition. Mobile subscription counts overstate people — multi-SIM inflates subscriptions well above unique subscribers, which is why the 52% unique-subscriber and 27% mobile-internet figures matter more than headline penetration. The 2025 WUENIC figures were reported as 2025 estimates; if they are in fact the July 2025 release of 2024 data, the year label shifts by one but the levels do not.

evidence.question: What is the observed lag between a demonstrated AI capability and a realised human benefit — is there any case where it has closed?
evidence.answer:
The best-documented closure is a rich-country screening programme, and it took about six years from capability to randomised evidence — with the outcome endpoint still not reported.

**The one strong case: mammography.** MASAI randomised 105,915 Swedish women between April 2021 and December 2022; final results published in The Lancet (Feb 2026) show sensitivity 80.5% vs 73.8% at identical specificity (98.5%), 12% fewer interval cancers (82 vs 93), 27% fewer aggressive (non-luminal A) cancers, a 29% higher cancer detection rate, and reduced reading workload. This is the strongest realised AI health benefit in existence. Note where it happened: a country with an organised population-based screening programme, universal invitation, and *two* radiologists reading every film — i.e. the benefit was substituting for an abundance of specialist labour. In most low-income countries population-based screening mammography does not exist at all; LMIC mammography screening rates run 5.6%–13%, and access within those countries is pro-rich in every country studied. The intervention that worked in Sweden has no delivery channel in Malawi.

**Drug discovery.** The compressed-21st-century claim has a scoreboard now. An ASCO 2026 analysis counted 117 AI-enabled therapeutic assets across 63 companies that had entered interventional human trials; 60 (51.3%) had completed Phase 1 and only 8 (6.8%) had completed Phase 2. Approvals: zero. The furthest-advanced case, a generative-AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, published a 71-patient Phase 2a in Nature Medicine (2025) and entered a 320-patient, 52-week Phase 3 in China. AlphaFold predicted ~200 million structures in 2022; four years on, the honest assessment in the trade literature is that it has changed structural biology far more than it has changed drug approval, and the DeepMind-affiliated therapeutics venture had not put a compound into humans as of early 2026. The trial clock has not been compressed by anything.

**Regulatory throughput versus deployment.** As of late March 2026 there were 1,524 FDA-authorised AI medical devices, 1,163 of them radiology (76%), with the agency clearing roughly 30 a month. But the only systematic study of *use* — 11 billion CPT claims, January 2018 to June 2023 — found adoption in the US 'still nascent and concentrated in a handful of devices'. Authorisation is not deployment; deployment is not benefit. And none of that machinery reaches poor countries: as of October 2025 only nine of 54 African countries had reached WHO Maturity Level 3 for *medicines* regulation, and device regulation lags behind that.

**The most likely near-term global win is not health.** AI weather prediction now beats the best physical models on most variables (GraphCast on 99.7% of tropospheric test variables vs ECMWF HRES; GenCast on 97.2% of targets beyond 36-hour lead times), costs almost nothing at inference, needs no trial and no regulator, and can ride existing SMS and radio channels. Africa has ~37 weather radars for 1.2 billion people at over $1M per station, and around 60% of the continent's population lacks effective early warning. That is a gate made of delivery, not of capability — exactly the kind an axis should be able to represent.
evidence.figures: MASAI (Lancet, Feb 2026): 105,915 women randomised Apr 2021–Dec 2022 (53,043 AI / 52,872 control); sensitivity 80.5% vs 73.8%; specificity both 98.5%; interval cancers 82 vs 93 (−12%); −27% non-luminal A; +29% cancer detection rate. LMIC mammography screening rates: 5.58%–12.96%; population-based screening mammography unavailable in most of sub-Saharan Africa. AI-enabled drugs (ASCO 2026): 117 assets, 63 companies in interventional trials; 60 (51.3%) completed Phase 1; 8 (6.8%) completed Phase 2; 0 approved. Rentosertib/ISM001-055: 71-patient Phase 2a (Nature Medicine 2025); Phase 3 recruiting 320 patients over 52 weeks in China. AlphaFold: ~200M structures predicted (2022). FDA-authorised AI devices: 1,524 total, 1,163 radiology (76.3%) as of late March 2026; 68 new radiology clearances in Q1 2026; ~30 clearances/month. US clinical adoption study: 11bn CPT claims Jan 2018–Jun 2023, adoption 'nascent and concentrated in a handful of devices' (NEJM AI, Jan 2024). African medicines regulators at WHO Maturity Level 3: 9 of 54 (Oct 2025). Weather: GraphCast beats ECMWF HRES on 99.7% of tropospheric test variables; GenCast beats ECMWF ENS on 97.2% of targets >36h; Africa has ~37 radars for 1.2bn people, >$1M/station; ~60% of Africa's population lacks effective early warning; AI early-warning deployment quoted at $1,430–$1,730/month nationally.
evidence.uncertainty: MASAI is a screening-accuracy trial; it does not report breast-cancer mortality, and interval-cancer reduction is a surrogate. The '117 assets / 8 completed Phase 2 / 0 approved' count comes from an ASCO 2026 analysis reported secondhand and I could not open the primary abstract — the counting rule for 'AI-enabled' is elastic and different analysts give different totals (one 2026 source counts 173 programmes). The AI weather cost figures ($1,430–1,730/month for national coverage) come from a single ResearchGate paper and should be treated as an advocacy estimate, not a costed procurement. The NEJM AI adoption study data ends June 2023 and predates the LLM deployment wave entirely.

evidence.question: What actually gates the arrival of gains, in observed order of bindingness?
evidence.answer:
From the evidence above, the gates stack in roughly this order, and they are largely *not* the gates a capability forecast would predict:

1. **A delivery channel that already exists.** Every realised benefit rode an existing pipe: mammography rode Sweden's screening programme; TB CAD rides X-ray machines and national TB programmes; the Kenya copilot rides an existing EHR at an existing clinic chain; the Nigeria tutoring trial rode schools with power and supervision. Where the pipe is absent, the capability sits unused — a diabetic-retinopathy model that beats specialists rejected 21% of images because Thai clinics had no darkenable room.

2. **Complementary physical capital and labour.** WHO's African Region has 1.55 health workers per 1,000 against a 4.45 threshold, with a projected 6.1 million shortfall by 2030. AI advice needs someone to act on it, and something to act with. This is why 'detection doubled' can be a null result for health.

3. **The judgement to use the output.** The Kenya entrepreneurs result is the cleanest demonstration: identical tool, identical advice, +15% for strong performers and −8% for weak ones, because the difference was in filtering. This gate does not open with better models; it opens with training, or with systems that constrain the output (the Kenya copilot's traffic-light design does exactly this — it only speaks when it detects an error).

4. **Trial and regulatory time, in medicine only.** Phase 2 and Phase 3 are the expensive, unpredictable stages and AI has not shortened them; the 52-week Phase 3 for the most advanced AI-discovered drug is a 52-week Phase 3. Nine of 54 African regulators are at WHO Maturity Level 3.

5. **Electricity, connectivity, devices, skills.** 730 million without power; a 3.1 billion usage gap; handsets at 48% of monthly income for the poorest quintile; 5% basic digital skills in low-income countries.

6. **Price and jurisdictional availability.** Real but currently the *least* binding of the six, given a 280x cost collapse and zero-price tiers reaching hundreds of millions in India. Availability blocks a handful of countries (DRC, Afghanistan, Eritrea, South Sudan, Chad, CAR, Yemen and others), which matters enormously to the people in them and little to the aggregate.

The direction of the whole list: benefits arrive first where a rich system already had a specialist to substitute for, and last where there was no system at all. That is the opposite ordering from need. It is also the ordering the historical base rate predicts — the Green Revolution reached 63% of developing-country cropland and skipped sub-Saharan Africa; smallpox was beaten in ten years because someone bought the delivery.
evidence.figures: Health workers per 1,000, WHO African Region: 1.55 vs 4.45 threshold; 6.1M shortfall by 2030 vs 11.8M needed; 4 of 47 countries above threshold. Thailand DR deployment: 21% of images rejected; ~10 patients per 2-hour session. Kenya entrepreneurs: +15% high performers, −8% low performers, same advice. African regulators at WHO ML3: 9 of 54 (Oct 2025). Electricity: 730M without (2024). Usage gap: 3.1bn (Sept 2025). Handset cost: 48% of monthly income for poorest quintile in LMICs. Digital skills: 5% in low-income countries (2023). Inference cost fall: 280x (Nov 2022–Oct 2024). Rural sub-Saharan African schools: ~33% without reliable electricity, >67% without dependable internet (WDR 2026).
evidence.uncertainty: The ordering is my synthesis, not any single source's finding, and it is inferred from a handful of well-documented cases that are not a random sample — successful deployments get written up and failures usually do not, so the 'existing pipe' pattern may be partly a publication artefact. The ranking would change under a capability discontinuity: if models became reliable enough to need no human filtering, gate 3 collapses and gate 2 weakens, and the whole list reorders. Nobody has tested that.

evidence.question: What is contested, and what is the credible range on each contested point?
evidence.answer:
**1. Is the AI access gap widening or narrowing?** Range: growing 4x faster in the poorest countries (OpenAI, May 2025) to growing 2x faster in the Global North (Daepp & Slaughter, May 2026). Unresolved. Levels are unambiguous (~50x on visits per internet user, May 2025); direction is not.

**2. How fast will AI-driven health benefits reach the poorest countries?** Range: ~50% within 5–10 years of powerful AI (Amodei, Oct 2024, explicitly lower-confidence than his biology claim) versus the historical base rate of 10–20 years for a *vaccine introduction* alone, 28 years for two-thirds Green Revolution adoption with sub-Saharan Africa excluded, and 144 years and counting for electricity. The gap between these is the axis's whole subject.

**3. Will AI compress drug development?** Range: 50–100 years into 5–10 (Amodei) versus the Derek Lowe-style position that Phase 2/3 human trials are the expensive, unpredictable failure point and AI touches the cheap end. Current scoreboard favours the sceptics: 117 assets in trials, 8 through Phase 2, 0 approved as of 2026. But the scoreboard is young — the oldest AI-discovered candidates are ~5 years into a 10–15 year pipeline, so the null is not yet informative either way.

**4. How large is the macro gain?** Range: <0.53%–0.66% TFP over 10 years (Acemoglu) to ~1pp annual labour-productivity growth (Aghion & Bunel, Filippucci et al.) — roughly tenfold. Most 2026 macro studies still find limited evidence of a significant aggregate AI effect.

**5. Does AI equalise or stratify within a country?** Range: −8% for low performers and +15% for high performers (Kenya, entrepreneurship) to +34% for novices and ~0 for experts (US call centre). Both credible, opposite signs. My read: verifiable-answer, scripted tasks equalise; open-ended judgement tasks stratify. That reconciliation is inference, not established.

**6. Is AI diffusing faster than previous general-purpose technologies?** The World Bank says yes (middle-income countries at half of ChatGPT traffic within six months versus 20 years for the internet to reach lower-income countries). The counter is that this compares a traffic share for *middle*-income countries against physical arrival for *lower*-income ones, and low-income countries were under 1% of that same traffic. Both statements are true of different populations; the axis should not let one stand for the other.
evidence.figures: Access-gap direction: +4x growth in lowest-income countries (May 2025) vs 2x faster growth in Global North in H2 2025 (May 2026). Health-benefit propagation: 50% in 5–10 years (Amodei) vs 10–20 yr vaccine introduction lag, 28 yrs to 63% Green Revolution adoption, 144 yrs and 730M still unelectrified. Drug pipeline: 117 assets / 60 through Phase 1 / 8 through Phase 2 / 0 approved (2026). Macro: 0.53–0.66% TFP over 10 yrs vs ~1pp/yr labour productivity. Within-country distribution: −8%/+15% (Kenya) vs +34%/~0 (call centre). Diffusion speed: 6 months to 50% of traffic from middle-income countries vs 20 years for internet to reach lower-income countries; low-income countries <1% of GenAI traffic.
evidence.uncertainty: Point 5's reconciliation is mine and should be labelled as a hypothesis in any prose that uses it. Point 3's scoreboard depends on a contested definition of 'AI-discovered' — counts in the public literature for 2026 range from 117 to 173 depending on inclusion criteria. On point 1, I could not find any third dataset to break the tie between the two vendor-derived claims.

evidence.question: What should the axis measure, and what would distinguish its positions?
evidence.answer:
The axis should measure a *dated, thresholded arrival of benefit to a named population*, because that is the only formulation the evidence can adjudicate and the only one immune to the letter-inherits-a-new-meaning failure this project has hit five times. Two design points from the research:

**Do not key positions to a binary 'do gains arrive'.** The evidence says gains arrive in a fixed order (rich system with an existing delivery pipe first, poor system with none last), so the informative variable is the *lag*, not the fact. A good position set differs on (a) which domain lands first, (b) the lag in years between capability and a measurable population-level benefit, and (c) whether the recipient population is high-income, middle-income or low-income. The rule 'one axis, one question' from the 2026-08-13 evidence programme applies hard here: 'whether' and 'where' are two questions and mixing them creates a world the axis cannot say.

**Anchor at least one position on a checkable claim.** Amodei's 'maybe 50% of AI-driven health benefits propagate to even the poorest countries within 5–10 years' of powerful AI is the best available anchor and is his own sentence. The historical base rate anchors the other end: vaccine introduction lag 10–20 years; Green Revolution 28 years to 63% and sub-Saharan Africa skipped; electricity 144 years and 730 million still waiting; smallpox — the single fastest global delivery ever achieved — 10 years of a fully funded campaign for a cheap, single-dose, unregulated intervention. Anything faster than smallpox is a claim that AI delivery beats the best delivery in human history.

**Candidate distinguishing questions for the positions**, each with a live witness available:
- Does an AI-attributable benefit show up in a *national health statistic* anywhere (any income group), and by when? Nothing does today.
- Does an AI-derived drug get approved, and where is it first available? 0 of 117 as of 2026; 8 have cleared Phase 2.
- Do the gains land in a domain with no trial and no regulator (weather, agronomy, education, logistics) before they land in medicine? Weather is the strongest candidate: capability already exceeds physical models, inference is near-free, ~60% of Africans lack effective early warning.
- Does the ratio of high-income to low-income use per internet user fall below 10x? It was ~50x in May 2025.
- Do the low-income countries get the benefit *without* getting the compute? Under 0.1% of global data-centre capacity is in low-income countries; the WDR 2026's 'adopt, adapt, advance' framing assumes yes.

**A caution on interactions.** This axis is not independent of D (diffusion and labour) or E (economy). The Kenya result implies that D's 'client-judged paid work done to standard' can rise while the gains axis moves *against* the poorest users. And a compute build-out that serves the axis positively (delivery capacity) also loads S. The axis is genuinely new — no existing control asks it — but it should be wired with conditionals to D, S and E, not left free-floating.

**Naming.** Keep the axis prose to 'the two or three United States frontier laboratories', 'Chinese frontier laboratories', 'the multilateral health funders', 'the largest Indian carrier'. All company names in the record above stay in the record.
evidence.figures: Anchors: Amodei 50% of health benefits to the poorest countries in 5–10 years post-powerful-AI (Oct 2024) → roughly 2031–2037 on a 2026–27 arrival. Base rates: smallpox 10 yrs of campaign (1967–77), vaccine introduction lag 10–20 yrs, Green Revolution 9%→63% in 28 yrs (1970–98) with SSA excluded, mobile internet 27% in SSA at 44 yrs, electricity 730M unserved at 144 yrs. Current state to beat: ~50x use gap per internet user (May 2025); <0.1% of data-centre capacity in low-income countries (June 2025); 4 of 86 AI health RCTs in LMICs (2018–2023); 0 of 117 AI-enabled drugs approved (2026); 1,524 FDA-authorised AI devices with 'nascent' clinical use.
evidence.uncertainty: This is design recommendation, not measurement. The specific position boundaries (which lag intervals, which income groups) are a judgement call I have not tested against the forecast's existing scoring machinery. The claim that weather lands before medicine is a hypothesis with good priors (no trial, no regulator, near-free inference, existing SMS/radio channels) but no realised-benefit evidence yet — no study I found measures lives or crop yield saved by AI forecasting in Africa. And the interaction claims (this axis vs D, S, E) are structural inferences from the control definitions given to me, not from anything in the sources.

evidence.question: Machine-designed drugs in trials: what has actually read out, at what phase, and with what result?
evidence.answer:
One molecule and one only has a peer-reviewed efficacy read-out where BOTH the target and the compound came from generative AI: rentosertib (formerly INS018_055/ISM001-055), a TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sponsored by Insilico Medicine. Be strict about what that Phase 2a was: a 71-patient, 12-week, 22-site trial in China (NCT05938920, run 19 Jun 2023 – 8 Aug 2024) whose PRIMARY endpoint was safety — the proportion of patients with at least one treatment-emergent adverse event. FVC was a SECONDARY endpoint. The widely-quoted '+98.4 mL' is a WITHIN-ARM mean change for the 60 mg QD group (95% CI 10.9 to 185.9), set beside −20.3 mL for placebo (95% CI −116.1 to 75.6). The paper reports no between-arm significance test for that comparison, the confidence intervals overlap heavily, and n=18 per arm. The authors' own conclusion is that the drug 'warrants further investigation in larger-scale clinical trials of longer duration'. Treatment discontinuations were driven by liver toxicity and diarrhoea.

The Phase 3 exists and is registered: NCT07687459, 320 patients, 47 centres, all in China, 52 weeks of dosing, primary endpoint the annual rate of FVC decline. Estimated start 30 Aug 2026; estimated primary completion 30 Oct 2029.

Elsewhere in the field: Recursion (post-Exscientia merger) discontinued REC-994 (cerebral cavernous malformation, 62 patients, met its safety primary endpoint but showed no meaningful clinical benefit) and REC-2282 (NF2), and shopped REC-3964 for out-licensing, in a May 2025 pipeline cull. Absci's ABS-101 (anti-TL1A, de novo generative design) dosed its first Phase 1 participants in May 2025. Insilico's ISM8969 entered Phase 1 (NCT07581431, 100 participants, recruiting from 15 Jun 2026). Isomorphic Labs — despite three years of expectation — had still not publicly confirmed a dosed patient as of mid-2026, and has no trial registered under its own sponsorship on ClinicalTrials.gov.
evidence.figures: Rentosertib Ph2a: N=71 (18/18/18/17), 12 weeks, TEAE rates 72.2%/83.3%/83.3% vs 70.6% placebo; FVC +98.4 mL (95% CI 10.9–185.9) at 60 mg QD vs −20.3 mL (95% CI −116.1–75.6) placebo. Published Nature Medicine 2025 Aug;31(8):2602–2610, online 3 Jun 2025 (PMID 40461817). Phase 3 NCT07687459: n=320, 47 sites (all China), 52 wk dosing, start 30 Aug 2026 (est), primary completion 30 Oct 2029 (est). Recursion cull: 3 programmes, May 2025.
sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40461817/ (Nature Medicine, 3 Jun 2025 — full abstract retrieved via NCBI E-utilities)
evidence.uncertainty: The rentosertib FVC result is a secondary endpoint in a safety trial with 18 patients per arm; it is a signal, not evidence of efficacy, and the sponsor authored the paper. Several secondary outlets (chemdiv, MLQ News) wrongly attribute ISM8969 to Isomorphic Labs; ClinicalTrials.gov and a EurekAlert release confirm ISM8969/HT-001 is Insilico's brain-penetrant NLRP3 inhibitor co-developed with Hygtia. Treat any 'Isomorphic dosed a patient' claim as unconfirmed.

evidence.question: Have any AI-discovered molecules been approved?
evidence.answer: No. As of 20 August 2026 there is no marketing authorisation anywhere in the world — FDA, EMA or NMPA — for a molecule whose discovery is attributed to AI. This is the single hardest fact in the whole subject and it should anchor the axis. Note the definitional trap: regulators do not maintain an 'AI-discovered' category, so the claim is only as good as the industry trackers' classification, and those trackers disagree about which molecules count (target found by AI? compound designed by AI? both?). Rentosertib is the most advanced and most defensible candidate for 'first', and its pivotal read-out is scheduled for late 2029, which puts a plausible first approval in 2030–31 — not the 2026 or 2027 that trackers have been predicting, and sliding, for three consecutive years. Regulatory designations held are real but do not shorten the trial: FDA Orphan Drug Designation (Feb 2023) and China CDE Breakthrough Therapy Designation (May 2025).
evidence.figures: 0 approvals worldwide as of Aug 2026. Rentosertib pivotal primary completion Oct 2029. Predicted-first-approval dates from trackers: 2026 → 2027 → 2027–28 across successive years. FDA CDER approved 46 novel drugs in 2025 (34 NMEs, 12 biologics); none AI-attributed.
evidence.uncertainty: 'Zero approvals' rests on the absence of a positive claim rather than on a regulator's register, because no regulator tracks the category. A generously-defined 'AI-assisted' claim could be attached retrospectively to approved drugs where ML was used somewhere in the pipeline; that claim would be unfalsifiable and should be refused.

evidence.question: AI-enabled medical devices: how many are authorised, and what are they actually for?
evidence.answer:
This is where AI has genuinely arrived, and it is almost entirely one specialty doing one thing. I parsed the FDA's own AI-Enabled Medical Device List directly: 1,524 entries, the most recent decision dated 30 March 2026. Radiology holds 1,164 of them — 76.4%. Cardiovascular is 147, neurology 70, and everything else is a long tail in single or double digits (ophthalmic 10, pathology 9, dental 5). The regulatory route matters more than the count: 1,466 (96.2%) came through 510(k) substantial-equivalence, 39 through De Novo, 19 through PMA. A 510(k) clearance turns on equivalence to a predicate device, not on a demonstration that patients do better.

What they do is overwhelmingly image reconstruction, triage, measurement and detection support — CT and MR reconstruction engines, ejection-fraction and aortic-stenosis measurement, stroke and pneumothorax triage, contouring for radiotherapy planning. These are workflow instruments. The FDA states plainly that it has not yet tagged which devices contain foundation models or LLMs and will 'explore methods' to do so — meaning that as of the list's cut-off no authorised device is publicly identified as generative-AI-based.

The growth curve: 65 authorisations in 2018, 235 in 2024, 333 in 2025, and 92 in Q1 2026 (69 of those radiology).

By panel: Radiology 1,164 (76.4%), Cardiovascular 147, Neurology 70, Anesthesiology 26, Gastro-Urology 25, Hematology 21, Ophthalmic 10, Pathology 9. By pathway: 510(k) 1,466 (96.2%), De Novo 39, PMA 19. By year of decision: 2018 65, 2019 80, 2020 114, 2021 130, 2022 162, 2023 226, 2024 235, 2025 333, 2026-to-cutoff 92.

evidence.uncertainty: The FDA states the list is not comprehensive — it is built by string-matching AI terms in public decision summaries, so it both misses devices whose summaries do not say 'AI' and cannot distinguish a genuine learned model from a marketing adjective. The list is also stale: its most recent entry is 30 March 2026, roughly five months before today, so Q2 2026 authorisations are not yet reflected.

evidence.question: Structural biology: what did AlphaFold change downstream?
evidence.answer:
The capability is real and enormous; the downstream therapeutic benefit is, five years on, still not demonstrable in a single approved or even late-stage medicine. DeepMind's own five-year retrospective (25 November 2025) claims over 3 million researchers in 190+ countries, more than a million users in low- and middle-income countries, 200 million+ predicted structures, 8 million+ folds through AlphaFold Server, 35,000+ citations of the paper and 200,000+ papers incorporating elements of AlphaFold 2. It cites an independent finding that AlphaFold 2 users increased their submission of novel EXPERIMENTAL structures by over 40% — a genuinely important result, because it means prediction pulled experiment rather than replacing it — and that AlphaFold-linked work is twice as likely to be cited in clinical articles.

What that retrospective does not contain is a single named drug or clinical candidate arising from AlphaFold. That absence, in a document written to make the strongest case, is the most informative thing in it. The mechanism of benefit so far is upstream: druggability assessment and virtual screening for targets that had no experimental structure at all, and faster molecular replacement in crystallography. Isomorphic Labs, founded in 2021 on exactly this bet and holding roughly $2.7bn of outside capital, had no dosed patient as of mid-2026.
evidence.figures: DeepMind retrospective, 25 Nov 2025: >3m researchers, >190 countries, >1m users in LMICs, 200m+ structures, 8m+ folds via AlphaFold Server, 35,000+ citations, 200,000+ derivative papers, >40% increase in novel experimental structure submissions by AF2 users, ~2× clinical citation rate, >30% of AlphaFold-related research disease-focused. Named clinical candidates arising: 0.
evidence.uncertainty: The '>40% more experimental structures' figure comes via DeepMind citing an independent analysis; I did not read the underlying study. Absence of a named AlphaFold-derived clinical candidate in a corporate blog is suggestive, not conclusive — structure prediction is now so diffuse a step that attribution to it would rarely be claimed even where it mattered.

evidence.question: Is there any MEASURED change in a health outcome attributable to AI?
evidence.answer:
There are two, and exactly two, that survive scrutiny — and neither is what the discourse assumes.

First, and strongest: an AI-ECG mortality alert. A pragmatic multisite RCT in Taiwan (39 physicians, 15,965 patients, NCT05118035) flagged hospitalised patients predicted to be at high risk of death. It met its primary endpoint: 90-day all-cause mortality 3.6% in the intervention arm vs 4.3% in control, HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.70–0.99). In the prespecified high-risk-ECG subgroup, HR 0.69 (0.53–0.90), and cardiac death 0.2% vs 2.4% (HR 0.07, 95% CI 0.01–0.56). The authors state openly that the means by which the alert reduced mortality are 'to be fully elucidated'. Nature Medicine, April 2024. Single health system; not replicated at scale that I could find.

Second, and more contested than its press coverage: MASAI, the first RCT of AI-supported population mammography screening, final primary results in The Lancet, 31 January 2026. 105,934 Swedish women randomised April 2021 – December 2022. Interval cancer rate 1.55 vs 1.76 per 1,000 — proportion ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.65–1.18, p=0.41). That is a NON-INFERIORITY result. The 12% reduction reported everywhere is the point estimate of a null finding. What IS statistically significant is sensitivity: 80.5% vs 73.8% (p=0.031), with identical specificity of 98.5%, and a previously-reported 44% cut in screen-reading workload. Descriptively, fewer interval cancers were invasive (75 vs 89), T2+ (38 vs 48) or non-luminal A (43 vs 59). So: more cancers caught at screening, less radiologist labour, same false positives — and no demonstrated reduction in interval cancer, let alone in mortality, which would take decades to measure.

Against those, the field-wide picture is thin. A scoping review of every RCT of AI in clinical practice (Lancet Digital Health, May 2024, Topol and Rajpurkar among the authors) found 86 trials, 81% reporting positive primaries — but the primaries were overwhelmingly diagnostic yield and performance, not patient outcomes, and the trials were predominantly single-centre with likely publication bias. My own query of ClinicalTrials.gov on 20 August 2026 found 1,978 interventional studies mentioning artificial intelligence, of which 599 are completed but only 76 (3.8%) have results posted, and only 74 name mortality anywhere in their outcomes.
evidence.figures: AI-ECG RCT (Nature Medicine, Apr 2024, NCT05118035): 15,965 patients, 90-day mortality 3.6% vs 4.3%, HR 0.83 (0.70–0.99); high-risk subgroup HR 0.69 (0.53–0.90); cardiac death 0.2% vs 2.4%, HR 0.07 (0.01–0.56). MASAI (Lancet, 31 Jan 2026, NCT04838756): 105,934 women, interval cancer 1.55 vs 1.76/1,000, PR 0.88 (0.65–1.18) p=0.41; sensitivity 80.5% vs 73.8% p=0.031; specificity 98.5% both arms; prior reported 44% reading-workload reduction and 29% higher cancer detection rate. Lancet Digital Health scoping review (May 2024): 86 RCTs, 70 (81%) positive primary. ClinicalTrials.gov, 20 Aug 2026: 1,978 interventional AI studies; 599 completed; 76 with posted results; 74 mentioning mortality.
evidence.uncertainty: The AI-ECG trial is one health system in Taiwan with an unexplained mechanism; a null replication would substantially weaken the only mortality result the field has. My ClinicalTrials.gov counts use a free-text term match, so they over-count studies that merely mention AI and under-count those that call it something else; and registry results-posting is a poor proxy for publication. MASAI's press framing (a '12% reduction in interval cancer') should be treated as unsupported: p=0.41.

evidence.question: Bottleneck 1 — trial length. How long is it, and did AI shorten it?
evidence.answer:
AI compressed the step before the trial and left the trial itself untouched. Run the rentosertib arithmetic, because it is the best case the field has: Insilico says it reaches preclinical candidate nomination in 12–18 months on average. Phase 1 ran Feb–Dec 2022. Phase 2a ran Jun 2023 – Aug 2024 and published Jun 2025. Phase 3 starts Aug 2026 and reads out Oct 2029, with approval plausibly 2030–31. So a discovery step compressed to roughly 18 months sits inside a development arc still running about a decade. The clock that AI stopped was never the long clock.

The generic figures behind that: Phase 1 ~1.5 years, Phase 2 ~2.5 years, Phase 3 3–4 years, 10–15 years discovery to approval, with overall Phase-1-to-approval probability of success stabilised around 5–10%. The pivotal trial for a slowly-progressive disease is irreducibly as long as the disease is slow — rentosertib's Phase 3 measures FVC decline over 52 weeks because that is how long it takes IPF to declare itself. No amount of model capability shortens a year of lung function.

The same holds on the device side, which is supposed to be the fast one: MASAI randomised its first woman in April 2021 and published its primary outcome in January 2026 — four years and nine months, for a screening aid that was already CE-marked when the trial began.
evidence.figures: Rentosertib arc: PCC nomination 12–18 months (sponsor claim) → Ph1 Feb–Dec 2022 → Ph2a Jun 2023–Aug 2024, published Jun 2025 → Ph3 Aug 2026–Oct 2029 → approval ~2030–31. Generic: Ph1 ~1.5 yr, Ph2 ~2.5 yr, Ph3 3–4 yr; 10–15 yr end to end; ~5% Ph1-to-approval success across 20,000+ programmes. MASAI: first randomisation Apr 2021 → primary publication Jan 2026 (4 yr 9 mo).
evidence.uncertainty: The generic phase durations come from secondary aggregators rather than a single primary dataset (Tufts CSDD and BIO/Citeline analyses sit behind paywalls); they are conventional and uncontroversial but should be cited as approximate. The 12–18 month PCC figure is the sponsor's own claim about its own platform.

evidence.question: Bottleneck 2 — recruitment. What is the evidence AI helps?
evidence.answer:
Recruitment is the most-cited operational bottleneck (widely reported as ~80% of trials delayed by patient-finding, with site contracting and budget negotiation the top causes of activation delay), and it is the place where AI's help is most plausible and least demonstrated. The best peer-reviewed system is TrialMatchAI (Nature Communications, 25 March 2026): an open-source LLM pipeline that retrieved at least one relevant trial in the top-20 for 92% of oncology patients, with >90% expert-validated accuracy at criterion-level eligibility classification.

Read that carefully. It measures RETRIEVAL accuracy. It does not measure whether a trial finished sooner or whether a patient was enrolled. The dramatic figures in circulation — screening cut from 8 hours to 30 minutes, '170× speed improvement', 'site screening from 6 months to 2 weeks', 'enrolment rates improved 65%' — are vendor marketing without a controlled comparator, and should not be carried into a forecast. To my knowledge no randomised or controlled evaluation has yet shown an AI matching tool shortening time-to-full-enrolment for a trial.
evidence.figures: TrialMatchAI (Nat Commun 2026;17:4472, 25 Mar 2026): 92% of oncology patients had ≥1 relevant trial in top-20; >90% criterion-level accuracy. Vendor claims (uncontrolled): 8 h → 30 min screening (94% reduction), 3× faster matching, 165–1,329 reviewer-hours saved, 6 months → 2 weeks site screening, +65% enrolment. Recruitment delay base rate: ~80% of trials; site-activation blockers: budget negotiation 72%, contract finalisation 60%, 66% of sites report contract/budget delays 'often' or 'always' (ICON 2025 site survey).
evidence.uncertainty: The vendor figures are the weakest material in this whole research pass — single-site, self-reported, no control arm. Flag them as contested or drop them. The ICON site-survey percentages come via a secondary summary; I did not read the survey instrument.

evidence.question: Bottleneck 3 — regulatory review. How long, and what is being done?
evidence.answer:
Review is the shortest of the gates and therefore the least worth optimising, which is why the recent activity there is more political signal than throughput gain. Standard FDA review runs 10–12 months, priority review 6–8; CDER approved 46 novel drugs in 2025, half of them for rare diseases, with 50% using an expedited pathway. Compare that to the 3–4 years of a Phase 3 and the ranking is obvious.

Three live interventions:
(1) The Commissioner's National Priority Voucher pilot, launched 17 June 2025, targets a review of 1–2 months against the usual 10–12. By early 2026 it had granted 15 vouchers, expanding toward 18. Four went to companies that had negotiated most-favoured-nation pricing deals with the President, and the programme is under congressional investigation by Pallone and Sanders — so it is a political instrument with a throughput side-effect, and its durability is uncertain.
(2) Elsa, the FDA's internal generative assistant built on Claude, deployed June 2025 and upgraded to a 4.0 agentic version by May 2026. It has been reported generating false citations and hallucinated data, and is not used in formal regulatory assessments.
(3) The animal-testing roadmap (10 April 2025) and its one-year progress report (20 April 2026) — the most substantive of the three. FDA has issued draft guidance reducing or eliminating non-human-primate testing for monoclonal antibodies (December 2025), expanded weight-of-evidence acceptance of New Approach Methodologies including computational toxicology, and — the milestone that matters for this axis — 'qualified the first artificial intelligence-based drug development tool'. PathAI's AIM-MASH AI Assist became the first AI pathology tool qualified under the Biomarker Qualification Program (December 2025), for use in MASH trials; CDER accepted the first in-silico DDT Letter of Intent into ISTAND in June 2026, an AI-driven digital liver model for predicting drug-induced liver injury.

Qualification is the mechanism to watch: it lets ANY sponsor use a validated tool in a defined context without re-validating it, which is how a model stops being one company's asset and becomes infrastructure.
evidence.figures: Standard FDA review 10–12 months; priority 6–8. CNPV target 1–2 months; launched 17 Jun 2025; 15 vouchers granted by early 2026, expanding to 18; 4 tied to MFN pricing deals; under congressional investigation. CDER 2025: 46 novel drugs (34 NMEs, 12 biologics), 50% expedited. Elsa deployed Jun 2025, v4.0 by May 2026; documented hallucinated citations. Animal-testing roadmap 10 Apr 2025; year-1 report 20 Apr 2026; first AI DDT qualified Dec 2025 (PathAI AIM-MASH, MASH trials); first in-silico ISTAND LOI accepted Jun 2026 (AI digital liver model for DILI); horseshoe-crab endotoxin transition could spare >1m animals/yr.
evidence.uncertainty: CNPV voucher counts (15 vs 18) differ across secondary sources and the pipeline is moving; the programme's entanglement with drug-pricing negotiations makes its survival across an administration change genuinely uncertain. Elsa's error rate has never been published — the criticism is from law firms and trade press, not from a measured evaluation.

evidence.question: Bottleneck 4 — the gate nobody counts: reimbursement and deployment
evidence.answer:
This is the finding I would build the axis around, because it is the gate that separates 'authorised' from 'anyone receives it' and almost no forecast models it. Set the numbers side by side. The FDA has authorised 1,524 AI-enabled devices. As of January 2026 there were 26 CPT codes for clinical AI services in total, of which just THREE are permanent Category I codes — FFR-CT, a CT-based cardiovascular risk service, and a diabetic-retinopathy detection tool. The other 23 are temporary Category III codes with no guaranteed payment rate and no clear route to permanence. In April 2025, 19 HCPCS codes existed for software-as-a-service billed as physician services, and NONE was billed more than 3,600 times or exceeded $200,000 in annual payments. Four SaaS tools held New Technology Add-On Payment status in 2025, up from one in 2023. The Bipartisan Policy Center's February 2026 brief puts the cause plainly: AI often does not fit Medicare's statutory benefit categories at all, so it is not separately reimbursed.

Deployment is real but shallow and unevenly distributed. ASTP/ONC Data Brief No. 80 (September 2025), drawn from the AHA IT supplement with a 51% response rate, found 71% of US non-federal acute care hospitals using EHR-integrated predictive AI in 2024, up from 66% in 2023 — but 86% among health-system-affiliated hospitals against just 37% among independents, with lower adoption in small, rural, government-owned and critical-access facilities. So the diffusion of the capability is itself a distributional fact: the hospitals whose patients are most underserved are the ones least likely to have it.
evidence.figures: 1,524 FDA-authorised AI devices vs 26 clinical-AI CPT codes (Jan 2026), of which 3 Category I and 23 Category III. April 2025: 19 SaaS HCPCS codes billed as physician services, none >3,600 times or >$200,000/yr; 19 hospital-outpatient SaaS codes. NTAP: 4 SaaS tools in 2025, 1 in 2023. 2026 OPPS final rule establishes national payment for AI-assisted cardiac analysis; MPFS Category I code with ~$1,000 payment for coronary plaque analysis. ASTP Data Brief No. 80 (Sep 2025): predictive AI use 66% (2023) → 71% (2024); health-system-affiliated 86% vs independent 37%; n=2,425 (2023), 2,080 (2024), 51% response rate.
evidence.uncertainty: The 1,524-vs-26 comparison is rhetorically powerful but not apples-to-apples: many authorised devices are reconstruction or measurement features bundled into scanner purchases and were never intended to be separately billed. The honest version of the claim is that separately reimbursed AI is a tiny and slow-growing subset, not that 1,498 devices are unpaid. ASTP's 51% response rate leaves room for adoption over-reporting by enthusiastic respondents.

evidence.question: Bottleneck 5 — manufacturing and physical supply
evidence.answer:
Weakest evidence base of the five, and worth saying so rather than filling with vendor copy. The recurring constraints named across 2025–26 trade reporting are sterile fill-finish capacity, viral-vector suites, high-potency API infrastructure, and — specifically for gene therapy — upstream supply of GMP-grade plasmid DNA, where a delay cascades through everything downstream. A 2026 industry survey reported 55.9% of respondents having difficulty finding gene-therapy CDMOs and 55.6% for cell therapy, with CDMOs projecting average five-year mammalian-cell-culture capacity expansion of 40.4% (up from 33.8% projected in 2025). A startup needing GMP capacity today waits months for a slot.

The structural point for the axis is one Amodei himself concedes: a new large-scale biologics plant takes years to build and qualify, and no model shortens concrete, stainless steel and regulatory qualification of a facility. Where a therapy is a small molecule the constraint is mild; where it is a cell or gene therapy — which is where much of the 'cure' rhetoric points — the manufacturing constraint may bind harder than the trial.
evidence.figures: 2026 CDMO survey: 55.9% report difficulty sourcing gene-therapy CDMOs, 55.6% cell therapy; projected 5-yr capacity expansion mammalian cell culture 40.4% (2026) vs 33.8% (2025); cell therapy 28.4% of CMOs, gene therapy 25%.
evidence.uncertainty: All figures here are trade-press and vendor surveys with undisclosed sampling. I would not put a number on manufacturing lead time in published prose; state the mechanism and the direction only. This is a genuine gap worth a dedicated research pass.

evidence.question: What does 'Machines of Loving Grace' actually claim, and what does it concede?
evidence.answer:
Read as written, the essay is more careful than its reception. Amodei's core claim (October 2024) is compressing 50–100 years of biological progress into 5–10 years after powerful AI — the 'compressed 21st century' — across five areas: biology and physical health; neuroscience and mental health; economic development and poverty; peace and governance; work and meaning. The specific health claims are reliable prevention and treatment of nearly all natural infectious disease; 95%-or-more reduction in cancer incidence and mortality; prevention of Alzheimer's; and a doubling of human lifespan to roughly 150 years. For development, a 20% annual GDP growth rate in the developing world for 5–10 years.

His own stated limiting factors are the load-bearing part and are usually dropped: the 'speed of the outside world' ('experiments on them take a certain amount of time which may be irreducible'), absent raw data ('in its absence more intelligence does not help'), intrinsic complexity and chaos, human constraints ('many things cannot be done without breaking laws, harming humans, or messing up society'), and physical law. On trials specifically he allows roughly one year end-to-end for a drug even under optimistic parallelisation.

He has since walked the tempo back himself. At a STAT event on 6 July 2026 he said he does not think progress can currently be made at a rate of ten years per year, and that his vision might not become visible for a decade. On 16 August 2026 he said 'AI will cure cancer' has become a cliché that reads as deceptive, conceded that AI companies including his own 'haven't yet delivered', and promised 'early glimmers' within months. Note what that concession is: an admission about the RATE, not a retraction of the destination.

The substantive counter-argument, from Niko McCarty (Asimov Press, 1 November 2024), is that the binding constraints are biophysical rather than computational — DNA cloning takes a week, human cells divide once a day — and that better models require better datasets which require solving wet-lab problems first, a chicken-and-egg that intelligence alone does not break. The sharpest institutional counter is the Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Perspective of 7 August 2026 by Bender, Scannell and 20 co-authors: 'evidence of their clinically relevant impact is, so far, disappointingly limited.' Scannell is the author of Eroom's Law; this is the field's own senior verdict, published two weeks ago.
evidence.figures: MoLG (Oct 2024): 50–100 years of biology in 5–10; cancer incidence/mortality −95%+; lifespan ~2× to ~150 yr; 20%/yr developing-world GDP growth for 5–10 yr; ~1 year end-to-end per drug even optimistically. Amodei, STAT, 6 Jul 2026: 'I don't think that today we can make progress at a rate of 10 years per year' (as reported). Amodei, 16 Aug 2026: companies 'haven't yet delivered', 'early glimmers' within months. NRDD Perspective, 7 Aug 2026, 22 authors, PMID 42567977.
evidence.uncertainty: The STAT quote is behind STAT+ and I read it only through a search summary of statnews.com — treat the wording as reported rather than verified verbatim. The August 2026 remarks come from finance-wire aggregators summarising a post on X; the substance is consistent across four outlets but no primary text was retrieved.

evidence.question: What is contested, and what is the range?
evidence.answer:
Four live disputes, each with a defensible span:

(1) HOW MANY AI-derived molecules are in the clinic. BCG/Wellcome counted 73–75 in 2023 (Jayatunga et al., Drug Discovery Today, June 2024). 2026 trackers claim 173 clinical programmes; one claims 200+; a figure of 117 assets across 63 companies is attributed to an ASCO 2026 analysis. The spread is a definitional artefact — 'AI-discovered target', 'AI-designed compound', 'AI used somewhere' are three different populations. Range: roughly 100–200, with the strict both-ends-AI definition yielding a handful.

(2) WHETHER AI improves the odds. BCG's finding — Phase 1 success 80–90% against an industry baseline of ~50–65%, collapsing to ~40% in Phase 2, in line with industry — is the most-cited number in the field and implies overall Phase-1-to-approval probability rising from 5–10% to 9–18%. That is a near-doubling of R&D productivity IF it holds. Derek Lowe's objection is that of 67 molecules from AI-discovery companies in trials in 2023, only 24 were aimed at 'AI-discovered' targets, and many of those targets were already known and already had drugs against them. His summary of himself: 'short-term pessimist, long-term optimist'. The structural reading that fits both: AI is good at the chemistry (Phase 1 measures whether the molecule behaves), and has not yet touched the biology (Phase 2 measures whether the target was right).

(3) WHERE the frontier is. China ran more clinical trials than the US in 2025 on some counts (~7,700 vs ~6,200), and NMPA's default IND clearance runs on the order of 60 working days against a pre-2015 baseline of 500+ days. Both the flagship AI drug's Phase 3 (47 sites, all China) and 24 of the 86 AI RCTs in the 2024 scoping review sit outside the US. If the gains land first, they may well land in Chinese and Northern European health systems, not American ones.

(4) WHEN the first approval comes. 2027–28 from optimistic trackers; 2030–31 if you simply read the rentosertib Phase 3 completion date and add a review cycle. I would weight the arithmetic over the tracker.
evidence.figures: Molecules in clinic: 73–75 (BCG, 2023) → 117 (ASCO 2026, unverified) → 173 (2026 trackers) → 200+ (one claim). Success rates (BCG/Jayatunga, Drug Discovery Today, Jun 2024): Ph1 80–90% vs 50–65% industry; Ph2 ~40%, at industry level; overall Ph1-to-approval 5–10% → 9–18%. Lowe: 24 of 67 AI-company molecules in 2023 aimed at AI-discovered targets. China: ~7,700 trials in 2025 vs ~6,200 US; NMPA IND ~60 working days (~87 calendar days claimed) vs >500 days pre-2015. First approval: 2027–28 (trackers) vs 2030–31 (arithmetic).
sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S135964462400134X (Jayatunga et al., Drug Discovery Today, Jun 2024)
evidence.uncertainty: I could not retrieve the Jayatunga full text (ScienceDirect 403) — the success-rate figures come through multiple consistent secondary summaries, which is adequate for a range but not for a headline number. The 117-asset ASCO 2026 figure I could NOT verify and would not publish. The China trial-count comparison comes from a low-quality source and should be re-derived from registries before use; note also that ClinicalTrials.gov systematically undercounts China because many trials register only on ChiCTR.

evidence.question: Where do the gains land, and how long is the lag to the last person?
evidence.answer:
The geography is not incidental — it is the axis's second dimension. Look at where each realised benefit actually landed. The only mortality RCT: one hospital system in Taiwan. The only population screening RCT: Sweden, 105,934 women. The 1,524 authorised devices: the United States, 76% of them radiology, concentrated in large health systems (86% adoption) and thin in independent and rural hospitals (37%). The flagship AI drug's pivotal trial: 47 sites, all in China. AlphaFold's million-plus LMIC users: upstream research access, not treatment.

Against that, the hard distributional number, and it has not moved in forty years. Wouters and Kuha (Health Affairs, October 2024) tracked 119 essential medicines and 6,871 launches across 75 markets from 1982 to 2024: median time from first global launch to availability was 2.7 years in high-income countries, 4.5 in upper-middle, 6.9 in lower-middle and 8.0 years in low-income countries. Three-quarters of first launches happened in eight countries. The gap between richer and poorer countries 'remained largely unchanged over time'.

So the honest lag structure has three segments stacked: capability exists → authorised or approved (years, and for drugs a decade); authorised → paid for and deployed in a rich health system (the reimbursement gate, where 1,524 devices meet 3 permanent payment codes); deployed in rich systems → available in poor ones (a further 5+ years, historically immovable). A model that fixes only the first segment moves the date a person is better off by a fraction of what it moves the date a capability exists.

The counter-case, and it is a real one: WHO has recommended computer-aided detection on chest X-ray for TB screening since 2021 and doubled its list of recommended products from four to eight in June 2025. TB CAD is the clearest instance of an AI capability whose primary deployment is in low- and middle-income settings, and it works precisely because it substitutes for a scarce input — a radiologist — rather than adding a billable service on top of an abundant one.
evidence.figures: Wouters & Kuha, Health Affairs 2024;43(10):1410–1419 (PMID 39374462): 119 medicines, 6,871 launches, 75 markets, 1982–2024; median time to availability from first global launch 2.7 yr (high-income), 4.5 (upper-middle), 6.9 (lower-middle), 8.0 (low-income); 74% of first launches in 8 countries; gap unchanged over time. WHO TB CAD: recommended since 2021, recommended products 4 → 8 in June 2025. Hospital AI adoption: 86% health-system-affiliated vs 37% independent (ASTP, 2024 data).
evidence.uncertainty: The Wouters data is pre-AI and describes medicines, not software; software could in principle diffuse faster because marginal cost is near zero. But the binding constraints on LMIC access are registration, procurement and health-system capacity, none of which marginal cost relieves — so I would treat the 5-year rich-to-poor lag as a reasonable prior with genuine upside for software specifically. The WHO product count (4→8) comes from advocacy-group reporting of the June 2025 policy update; the underlying WHO document was not retrieved.

evidence.question: Does deployed AI ever make outcomes WORSE, and does the forecast need that direction?
evidence.answer:
Yes, and this is the finding that keeps the axis from being a one-way ratchet. A multicentre observational study across four Polish endoscopy centres in the ACCEPT trial (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology, October 2025, published online 12 August 2025) compared the same endoscopists' unassisted performance three months before and three months after AI polyp-detection tools arrived. Adenoma detection rate in standard non-AI colonoscopy fell from 28.4% (226/795) to 22.4% (145/648), an absolute difference of −6.0% (95% CI −10.5 to −1.6, p=0.0089), with exposure to AI carrying an odds ratio of 0.69 in multivariable analysis. Since each 1% of ADR maps to roughly a 3% change in interval colorectal cancer risk, this is the first real-world evidence of automation-induced deskilling linked to a patient-relevant metric in medicine.

A second, subtler direction: verification burden. A systematic review and meta-analysis (JMIR, 4 August 2026; 21 studies, 2,885 professionals, 7 countries, PROSPERO-registered, GRADE-assessed) found ambient AI documentation reduced NASA-TLX temporal demand and effort with moderate certainty — but diagnostic imaging AI and clinical decision support showed 'mixed or paradoxically increased' workload, at very low certainty. The authors' conclusion is exact: 'Net benefit on the health care workforce remains an open empirical question.'

So the axis needs to be able to describe a world where capability rises, deployment rises, and the realised outcome moves sideways or down — because a deployed tool changes the human beside it, and the change is not always in the direction of the tool's own metric.
evidence.figures: Deskilling (Lancet Gastro Hep 2025;10(10):896–903, online 12 Aug 2025, PMID 40816301): 1,443 non-AI colonoscopies (795 before, 648 after); ADR 28.4% → 22.4%, absolute −6.0% (95% CI −10.5 to −1.6), p=0.0089; multivariable OR 0.69. Each 1.0% ADR ≈ 3.0% change in interval CRC risk. Workload meta-analysis (JMIR 2026;28:e93618, 4 Aug 2026): 21 studies, 2,885 professionals, 7 countries; ambient AI temporal demand SMD −1.46 (95% CI −2.81 to −0.11, k=2); imaging AI and CDSS mixed or increased, very low GRADE certainty.
evidence.uncertainty: The deskilling study is retrospective and observational with a three-month window, four centres, and an erratum; it establishes an association, not causation, and has not been replicated. The workload meta-analysis rests on k=2 or k=3 studies for its significant pooled estimates with prediction intervals crossing the null — the authors say so themselves.

evidence.question: What should the axis's positions actually differ on?
evidence.answer:
The evidence points to four discriminating variables, none of which is 'how good the models are'.

FIRST, WHICH SUBSTRATE. The realised gains split cleanly by whether the AI's output is an INFORMATION product or a MOLECULE. Information products — image reading, triage, risk alerts, documentation — reach patients in 1–4 years and already have two RCT-grade wins and 1,524 authorisations. Molecules reach patients in 10+ years and have zero approvals. Any position that treats 'biomedicine' as one thing will be wrong about half of it. A world where models get much better at biology but the trial system is unchanged looks, from a patient's point of view, almost exactly like today for a decade.

SECOND, WHICH GATE BINDS. Four candidates in rank order of duration: the pivotal trial (3–4 years, irreducible where the disease is slow), reimbursement and procurement (indefinite — 1,524 devices, 3 permanent payment codes), manufacturing (years for physical plant), regulatory review (10–12 months, already the shortest and already being cut to 1–2 by voucher). Positions should differ on which of these the world relaxes. Relaxing review changes almost nothing; relaxing the evidentiary standard for pivotal trials changes everything, and changes it in both directions.

THIRD, WHO RECEIVES. Rich health systems with a payment code; large hospital systems (86%) rather than independents (37%); Sweden, Taiwan, China, the US. Then a 5-year median lag to low-income countries that has not moved since 1982. The TB CAD case shows the exception worth naming: AI arrives fastest where it substitutes for a scarce human input rather than adding a billable service.

FOURTH, WHETHER ANYONE CAN TELL. This mirrors the A axis's 'and whether anyone can tell' and should be stated in the same register. Of 1,978 registered interventional AI studies, 76 have posted results. Of 86 published AI RCTs, most measured diagnostic yield rather than a patient outcome. Of 1,524 authorised devices, 96.2% cleared on predicate equivalence rather than an outcome demonstration. A world can be full of deployed, paid-for, apparently-working AI and contain no instrument capable of saying whether patients are better off — and the deskilling result shows that world can be silently negative.

One more design note, given this project's own history: key the positions to a MEASURED quantity — years of lag, number of gates cleared, share of population reached — not to a letter or a named domain. Domains get redefined; a lag in years survives a rebuild.
evidence.figures: Information-product lag ~1–4 yr (MASAI: Apr 2021 randomisation → Jan 2026 primary; devices: 510(k) in months). Molecule lag 10+ yr (rentosertib: ~2020 target → Oct 2029 pivotal → ~2030–31 approval). Gate durations: pivotal trial 3–4 yr; reimbursement indefinite (1,524 devices : 3 Category I codes); review 10–12 mo (→1–2 mo via CNPV). Receipt: 86% vs 37% hospital adoption; 2.7 yr vs 8.0 yr median availability high- vs low-income. Measurability: 76/1,978 registered AI trials with posted results; 96.2% of devices via 510(k).
evidence.uncertainty: This is synthesis, not evidence — it is my reading of what the evidence discriminates, and a different reading could weight the manufacturing gate higher than I have (I flagged that evidence as weak). The information/molecule split is clean today but could blur if generative models start producing devices whose approval requires outcome trials, which is the direction FDA's foundation-model tagging plans point.

evidence.question: What is the single most useful sentence-level framing for the reader's objection?
evidence.answer:
The reader's complaint was that a 2036 headline saying AI is 'wrong in ways found on the factory floor' sits oddly beside 'the machines keep getting better', and that improved capability should unlock benefits the forecast never names. The evidence says both halves of that headline can be true simultaneously and for a structural reason, not a rhetorical one: capability and benefit are separated by gates whose durations are set by biology, law and payment, none of which the models operate on.

The cleanest single demonstration is the one drug that worked. Insilico compressed target-to-candidate to 12–18 months — an unambiguous capability win. The resulting molecule's pivotal trial will read out in October 2029 because idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis takes 52 weeks to declare itself in a patient's lung function, and then 320 patients had to be found across 47 hospitals. The capability step got roughly ten times faster. The arc from target to a patient with a prescription stayed at about a decade.

And the field's own senior verdict, two weeks old at the time of writing: twenty-two authors in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery on 7 August 2026, including the author of Eroom's Law, asking 'where did we advance — and where are we yet to see impact — when it comes to what matters in drug discovery, which is to deliver safer and more efficacious medicines to patients faster', and answering that the evidence of clinically relevant impact is 'disappointingly limited'. Amodei himself, on 6 July 2026: not ten years per year, not yet. That is not a forecast of failure. It is a forecast that the benefit clock and the capability clock are different clocks — which is precisely the control the forecast is missing.
evidence.figures: Capability step: 12–18 months target-to-PCC. Benefit arc: ~2020 target → Oct 2029 pivotal read-out → ~2030–31 approval. NRDD verdict 7 Aug 2026: clinical impact 'disappointingly limited', 22 authors. Amodei 6 Jul 2026: not 10 years per year. AI-attributed drug approvals worldwide: 0. AI-enabled devices authorised: 1,524. Permanent Medicare payment codes for clinical AI: 3.
evidence.uncertainty: The framing generalises from biomedicine to the axis as a whole; logistics and other domains may have shorter gate structures and should be researched separately before the axis prose claims to cover them. The reader named logistics explicitly and I did not research it.
